'''''A Birch Grove''''' is a [[Landscape painting|landscape]] by the Russian artist [[Arkhip Kuindzhi]] (1842–1910), completed in 1879. It is kept in the [[Tretyakov Gallery|State Tretyakov Gallery]] (inventory 882). The size of the painting is {{convert|97|×|181|cm}}.<ref name=":0">Государственная Третьяковская галерея — каталог собрания / Я. В. Брук, Л. И. Иовлева. — М.: Красная площадь, 2001. — V. 4: Живопись второй половины XIX века, книга 1, А—М. — 528 p. —P. 330. — {{ISBN|5-900743-56-X}}.</ref><ref name=":1">Куинджи Архип Иванович — Берёзовая роща (HTML). [[Tretyakov Gallery|Государственная Третьяковская галерея]], www.tretyakovgallery.ru. Дата обращения: 8 June 2020. [https://web.archive.org/web/20200918194001/https://www.tretyakovgallery.ru/collection/berezovaya-roshcha/ Archive]: 18 September 2020.</ref> The canvas depicts [[birch]] trees growing in a sunny forest clearing.<ref name=":2">{{Harvard citation text|Мальцева|2001|p=52}}</ref> The unusual combinations of light and color and sharp contrast of sun and shadow create the impression of very bright sunlight.<ref name=":1" /> The upper parts of the birches are not shown; only the trunks and small branches are visible, which stand out in light green against the background of the dark green forest. The [[Composition (visual arts)|composition]] is divided into two parts by a stream running through the middle.<ref name=":2" />

Together with two other paintings by the artist (''[[:ru:После дождя (картина Куинджи)|After the Rain]]'' and ''[[:ru:Север (картина Куинджи)|North]]''), ''A Birch Grove'' was presented at the 7th Exhibition of the [[Peredvizhniki|Society of Travelling Art Exhibitions]] ("Peredvizhniki"), which opened in [[Saint Petersburg|St. Petersburg]] in February 1879.<ref name=":4">Товарищество передвижных художественных выставок. Письма, документы. 1869—1899 / В. В. Андреева, М. В. Астафьева, С. Н. Гольдштейн, Н. Л. Приймак. — М.: Искусство, 1987. — 668 p. — pp. 177–184.</ref><ref name=":5">{{Harvard citation text|Манин|1976|p=49}} </ref> The artist [[Ivan Kramskoi|Ivan Kramskoy]] reported that Kuindzhi's works were enthusiastically received by the public.<ref name=":6">{{Harvard citation text|Крамской И. Н. и Третьяков П. М.|1953|p=247|Ref=И. Н. Крамской и П. М. Третьяков}}</ref><ref name=":7">Товарищество передвижных художественных выставок. Письма, документы. 1869—1899 / В. В. Андреева, М. В. Астафьева, С. Н. Гольдштейн, Н. Л. Приймак. — М.: Искусство, 1987. — 668 p. — P. 186.</ref><ref name=":8">{{Harvard citation text|Чурак Г. С.|2018|pp=23—24|Ref=Чурак Г. С.}}</ref> In particular, the visitors to the exhibition noted the "extraordinary nature" of ''A Birch Grove''.<ref name=":9">{{Harvard citation text|Манин|1990|p=28}}</ref> Immediately after the exhibition, all three paintings were purchased by the Russian businessman [[Pavel Tretyakov]] for 6,500 rubles.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":10">Летопись жизни и творчества Архипа Ивановича Куинджи // Архип Куинджи / Т. Art critic [[Vladimir Stasov]] noted that ''A Birch Grove'' is a painting "with wonderfully illuminated trees and grass", and that in this work Kuindzhi "takes notes of strong spectacular lighting, which no one has tried before".<ref name=":17">{{Harvard citation text|Стасов В. В.|1968|p=170|Ref=Стасов В. В.}}</ref> Art historian Faina Maltseva wrote that ''A Birch Grove'' is an "innovative work" that is one of the best examples of realistic landscapes of the 1870s.<ref name=":2" /> According to the art historian Vitaly Manin, "there was no picture in Russian landscape painting where a bright sunny day was captured so joyfully and enlightened, where the artist's peaceful feeling was so fully expressed, where a bright sense of peace, uplifted mood received such a perfect embodiment".<ref name=":18">{{Harvard citation text|Манин|1976|p=50}}</ref>

==History==
===Previous events===
[[File:Kuindzhi Pine forest with a river 1878 grm.jpg|left|thumb|Arkhip Kuindzhi. ''Pine Forest with River'' (1878, State Russian Museum of Fine Arts)]]

From 1866 Arkhip Kuindzhi lived in [[Saint Petersburg|St. Petersburg]]. He worked in a photo studio as a retoucher, then began attending classes at the [[Imperial Academy of Arts|Academy of Arts]], and in 1868 received the title of [[Классный художник|non-class artist]].<ref>''М. ===The 7th Exhibition of the Association of Travelling Art Exhibitions===
[[File:Kuindzi by I.Kramskoy (1870s, RAN).jpg|thumb|[[Ivan Kramskoi|Ivan Kramskoy]]. Portrait of A. I. Kuindzhi (late 1870s, NIM RAH)]]

The canvas ''A Birch Grove'' was exhibited for the first time in 1879 at the 7th Exhibition of the Society of Travelling Art Exhibitions ("Peredvizhniki"), together with two other paintings by the artist: ''[[После дождя (картина Куинджи)|After the Rain]]'' and ''[[Север (картина Куинджи)|North]]''.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" /> The exhibition was opened on February 23, 1879 in St. Petersburg, where it lasted until March 25.<ref name=":15">{{Harvard citation text|Рогинская Ф. С.|1989|p=418|Ref=Рогинская Ф. С.}}</ref> The opening of the exhibition was delayed, mainly due to the unreadiness of Kuindzhi's landscapes. According to the artist Ivan Kramskoi, "the hall was being cleared, and Kuindzhi could not yet hang it, and it is too necessary to have it".<ref name=":16">Товарищество передвижных художественных выставок. Письма, документы. 1869—1899 / В. В. Андреева, М. В. Астафьева, С. Н. Гольдштейн, Н. Л. Приймак. — М.: Искусство, 1987. — 668 p. — P. 565.</ref> In a letter to [[Vasily Polenov]] dated February 18, Kramskoi reported, "Kuindzhi is delaying, and he has things that are too important to ignore".<ref>Товарищество передвижных художественных выставок. Письма, документы. 1869—1899 / В. В. Андреева, М. В. Астафьева, С. Н. Гольдштейн, Н. Л. Приймак. — М.: Искусство, 1987. — 668 p. — P. 176.</ref> The delay was a source of irritation for the organizers of the Moscow section of the touring exhibition — in a letter to Kramskoi on February 23, the artist [[Ilya Repin]] wrote: "Kuindzhi is not ready? Seven are not waiting for one; and it was very easy to add him after the opening".<ref name=":16" /> Kuindzhi's canvases appeared in the exhibition two days after its opening — on February 25.<ref name=":5" /> According to Kramsky, "Kuindzhi exhibited the paintings and did not spoil them, although he neither improved them".<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":7" />
[[File:Strekoza Kuindzhi Svet Yablochkova.jpg|left|thumb|[[Лебедев, Александр Игнатьевич|Alexander Lebedev]]. Kuindzhi. [[Yablochkov candle|Yablochkov Candle]] (caricature in the magazine ''[[Strekoza]]'', 1879)]]
The greatest impression was made by ''A Birch Grove'' — both artists and spectators who visited the exhibition noted "the extraordinary nature of the picture", which later became one of Kuindzhi's most famous works.<ref name=":9" /> Some of the artists' reviews of ''A Birch Grove'' are known from the words of contemporaries: Ivan Shishkin said: "This is not a painting, and from it you can write a picture...", and [[Vladimir Orlovsky]] admitted: "I never thought, never imagined that it was possible to bring the picture to such relief. It is not a picture, it is nature".<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Nevedomskiĭ, M. P.|Repin, I. E.|1997|p=100|Ref=NevedomskiĭMP}}</ref> In a letter to Pavel Tretyakov dated March 1, 1879, [[Ivan Kramskoi]] wrote about the reaction caused by the appearance of Kuindzhi's paintings at the exhibition: "The public received them enthusiastically, artists (that is, landscape artists) at the first moment dazed, they did not prepare, a long time were with open jaws and only now begin to gather their courage and then angrily, then secretly let various rumors and opinions, many reach a high comic in the denial of his paintings, so... cheers!"<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":7" /><ref name=":8" /> Some viewers suspected Kuindzhi of being a magician and believed the rumors that had spread that "the picture was painted on glass and illuminated from behind by a lamp".<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Зименко|1947|p=16}}</ref>

On March 15, the newspaper ''[[Novoye Vremya (newspaper)|Novoe Vremya]]'' (No. 1093, p. 4) published a detailed review by Vladimir Stasov entitled "Art Exhibitions of 1879", which praised Kuindzhi's "unusually poetic feeling and view" and also noted the originality of his paintings.<ref name=":10" /> Kuindzhi's popularity was also evidenced by [[Лебедев, Александр Игнатьевич|Alexander Lebedev's]] friendly [[caricature]] "Kuindzhi. [[Yablochkov candle|Yablochkov Candle]]", which was placed on the cover of the magazine ''[[Strekoza]]'' (No. 11, March 18, 1879) — the caricature depicted the artist standing next to ''A Birch Grove''.<ref name=":10" /><ref>{{Harvard citation text|Ефимова|2018|p=89}}</ref> Directly from the exhibition, all three of Kuindzhi's paintings, including ''A Birch Grove'', were bought from the artist by Pavel Tretyakov for 6,500 rubles.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":10" />

The Moscow part of the 7th Travelling Exhibition was opened on April 22, 1879.<ref name=":15" />  Shortly thereafter, the newspaper ''[[Молва (газета, 1879—1881)|Molva]]'' (No. 112, April 25, 1879) published an article "Brief notes (on reviews of art exhibitions and on the paintings of Mr. Kuindzhi)" signed by the pseudonym "Lubitel".<ref>Товарищество передвижных художественных выставок. Письма, документы. 1869—1899 / В. В. Андреева, М. В. Астафьева, С. Н. Гольдштейн, Н. Л. Приймак. — М.: Искусство, 1987. — 668 p. — P. 567.</ref> "Lubitel" spoke negatively about Kuindzhi's work and sharply criticized his paintings exhibited at the exhibition. In particular, he wrote: "Anyone who has ever observed in nature the relations of tones that give sunlight, who has ever studied the laws of transitions of one tone into another with different light effects, will agree that the light effects in Kuindzhi's paintings are exaggerated and completely wrong". As for the ''A Birch Grove'', "Lubitel" wrote that the trees in it do not grow, and "rastykana", they are "precisely cut out of cardboard, painted in a dirty-green shade and placed as a decoration".<ref>Товарищество передвижных художественных выставок. Письма, документы. 1869—1899 / В. В. Андреева, М. В. Астафьева, С. Н. Гольдштейн, Н. Л. Приймак. — М.: Искусство, 1987. — 668 p. — P. 568.</ref> In December 1879 it turned out that the author hiding behind the pseudonym "Lubitel" was one of the founding members of the organization of artist-pervizhniks, [[Mikhail Clodt von Jürgensburg|Mikhail Clodt]].<ref name=":10" /><ref>Архип Куинджи из собрания Русского музея / И. Н. Шувалова. — СПб.: Palace Editions, 2015. — 180 p. — pp. 12–13. — {{ISBN|978-5-93332-526-0}}.</ref> Angered by this act, Kuindzhi decided to withdraw from the partnership, which was finalized in early 1880. Thus, the 1879 exhibition presenting ''A Birch Grove'' became the last traveling exhibition with his participation.<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Гомберг-Вержбинская|1970|pp=167—168}}</ref>

===Later events===
[[File:Kuindzhi Birch grove version2 1881 c.jpg|thumb|Arkhip Kuindzhi. ''A Birch Grove'' (2nd variant, 1881, private collection)]][[File:Куинджи - Березовая роща 1901.jpg|left|thumb|Arkhip Kuindzhi. ''A Birch Grove'' (3rd variant, 1901, [[Belarusian National Arts Museum|The National Art Museum of the Republic of Belarus]])]]

In September 1880 Kuindzhi finished the painting ''[[Moonlit Night on the Dnieper]]''.<ref>Архип Куинджи из собрания Русского музея / И. Н. Шувалова. — СПб.: Palace Editions, 2015. — 180 p. — P. 13. — {{ISBN|978-5-93332-526-0}}.</ref> In October and November of the same year<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Манин|2000|p=23}}</ref> the painting was exhibited in the building of the [[Imperial Society for the Encouragement of the Arts|Society for the Encouragement of Artists]], on Bolshaya Morskaya Street in St. Petersburg, and it was the first time in the history of Russian art when the only painting was shown at the exhibition.{{Vague|date=May 2024}}<!--If what is meant is that no drawings, etchings, textiles, sculptures, etc were also shown, and that this was a first, then "the first time in the history of Russian art exhibitions when only paintings were shown". Or, of course with an entirely different meaning, "the first time in the history of Russian art exhibitions when only a single painting was shown" --><ref>{{Harvard citation text|Воронова|1986|p=106}}</ref>

In 1882, Kuindzhi organized another personal exhibition, which included three paintings: the second version of the canvas ''A Birch Grove'' (1881), the second version of the painting ''Night on the Dnieper'', as well as a new work, ''[[Днепр утром|Dnieper in the Morning]]'' (now in the State Tretyakov Gallery).<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Мальцева|1965|p=434}}</ref><ref name=":23">{{Harvard citation text|Мальцева|2001|p=55}}</ref> The exhibition was held in [[Пассаж Солодовникова|Solodovnikov's house]] on [[Kuznetsky Most]]<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Манин|1976|p=83}}</ref><ref>{{Harvard citation text|Сорокин В. В.|1991|p=91|Ref=Сорокин В. В.}}</ref><ref>{{Harvard citation text|Sorokin, V. V.|2006|p=84|Ref=SorokinVV}}</ref> and the paintings were displayed in daylight.<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Nevedomskiĭ, M. P.|Repin, I. E.|1997|p=135|Ref=NevedomskiĭMP}}

</ref> This exhibition turned out to be the last public exhibition in Kuindzhi's creative activity: until the end of his life he continued to create new works, but did not show them to the public.<ref name=":23" />

For a long time, almost nothing was known about Kuindzhi's new works. In 1901, he organized several private exhibitions, where four works were presented to close acquaintances: ''A Birch Grove'' (1901, now in the [[Belarusian National Arts Museum]]), a revised ''[[Evening in Ukraine]]'' (1878, completed in 1901, now in the GRM), ''Dnieper'' (1901, now in the [[Музеи Псковской области|Pskov Museum-Reserve]], a variant of the painting ''Dnieper in the Morning'', 1881) and ''[[Христос в Гефсиманском саду (картина Куинджи)|Christ in the Garden of Gethsemane]]'' (1901, now in the [[Vorontsov Palace (Alupka)|Vorontsov Palace-Museum]], [[Alupka]]).<ref name=":24">Притяжение земли // Архип Куинджи / Т. Л. Карпова, О. Д. Атрощенко, А. А. Ефимова. — М.: Государственная Третьяковская галерея, 2018. — pp. 63–120. — 360 p. — P. 100. — {{ISBN|978-5-89580-222-9}}.</ref>

Subsequently, ''A Birch Grove'' (the original version, created in 1879 and purchased by Pavel Tretyakov) was exhibited at a number of exhibitions, including the exhibition in the Tretyakov Gallery dedicated to the 25th anniversary of the death of P.M. Tretyakov (1923) and the exhibition of Russian art of the 18th–20th centuries (1957, Beijing). From 1971 to 1972 the canvas appeared in the exhibition ''Landscape Painting of the Peredvizhniki'' ([[Kiev]]<!--See WP:KIEV-->, Leningrad, Minsk, Moscow) on the occasion of the centenary of the [[Peredvizhniki|Society for Travelling Art Exhibitions]], in 1983–198{{Vague|date=May 2024}}<!-- Nineteen eighty when? --> — in the exhibition of the Academy of Arts of the USSR (Moscow); and in 1992, in the exhibition dedicated to the 150th anniversary of the birth of Kuindzhi (Moscow).<ref name=":0" /> It was also one of the exhibits of the exhibition of the works of Arkhip Kuindzhi, held from October 2018 to February 2019 in the technical building of the Tretyakov Gallery.<ref>''И. Владимиров.'' [https://rg.ru/2018/10/03/tretiakovskaia-galereia-pokazhet-retrospektivu-kuindzhi.html От заката до рассвета. Третьяковская галерея с 6 октября по 17 февраля покажет ретроспективу Куинджи] (HTML) (6 октября 2018). Дата обращения: 9 May 2020. [https://web.archive.org/web/20200105200142/https://rg.ru/2018/10/03/tretiakovskaia-galereia-pokazhet-retrospektivu-kuindzhi.html Archive]: 5 January 2020.</ref> {{As of|2020}}, the painting ''A Birch Grove'' was exhibited in room 21 of the main building of the Tretyakov Gallery on Lavrushinsky Lane.<ref name=":1" />

==Description==
''A Birch Grove'' is in the style of [[Romanticism|romantic]] landscape. As in other works by Kuindzhi, a significant effect is achieved by unusual combinations of light and color, sharp contrast of sun and shadow, which creates the impression of very bright sunlight.<ref name=":1" /> A forest clearing flooded with bright sunlight occupies the dominant position on the canvas. In the background, it is enclosed by dense, tall trees whose green silhouettes form a kind of living fence. The composition is divided into two parts by a stream running through the middle, covered with [[lemna]], and by the gap between the trees in the distance.<ref name=":2" /><ref>История русского искусства / М. Г. Неклюдова. — М.: Изобразительное искусство, 1980. — V. 2, book 1. — 312 p. — P. 80.</ref>[[File:Birch grove by Arkhip Kuindzhi in the State Tretyakov gallery IMG 7962 с.jpg|left|thumb|Painting ''A Birch Grove'' in the State Tretyakov Gallery]]The arrangement of the birches growing in the clearing in the foreground preserves this "accentuated symmetrical division of the compositional plans of the painting". The upper part of the birches is not shown, only their [[Trunk (botany)|trunks]] — brownish-greenish in the shade and bright white where they [[Face the Sun|face the sun]], and small branches with fresh leaves that stand out in light green against the dark green forest in the background. In the words of the artist [[Arkady Rylov]], "real is this joy that sparkles under the fragrant birches".<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Harvard citation text|Рылов А. А.|1954|p=46|Ref=Рылов А. А.}}</ref> The combination of different shades of green used in painting the birch foliage and the distant forest further emphasizes the feeling of a bright sunny day.

By cutting off the [[Crown (botany)|crowns]] of nearby trees, Kuindzhi narrows the space of the painting, depriving it of its [[Panoramic painting|panoramic]] character. As a result, the composition's character is more closed and intimate, with a weakening of its national content. At the same time, according to the art historian Vitaly Manin, "the universal content, which was created by a clearly expressed bright world view, optimism, brightly filling the picture with light, is intensified".<ref name=":25">{{Harvard citation text|Манин|1976|p=52}}</ref>

In general, the compositional solution of ''A Birch Grove'' corresponds to the [[Academic art|academic]] principles. This is particularly evident in the "backstage construction of the scene", where the trunks of the birch trees create the impression of a deep space, and the dark trees play the role of a theatrical [[Flat (theatre)|flat]]. Another academic technique is the use of traditional "triangles" formed by a lighted meadow, a bright sky, and a shaded stream; the apexes of these triangles converge at the intersection of the diagonals of the canvas. The well-considered linear construction is based on clear [[Perspective (graphical)|perspective]] cuts.<ref name=":25" /> The impression of natural depth of space is achieved by "the spectacular alternation of sunlight and dark shadow".<ref name=":3">{{Harvard citation text|Манин|1976|pp=52—53}}</ref>

A "[[Stereoscopy|stereoscopic]]" effect of painting is entirely determined by spatial construction, while "the interest in revealing the volumetric nature of the objects in ''A Birch Grove'' is clearly lost. The artist refuses the detailed development of [[Chiaroscuro|light and shadow transitions]], he "'collects' color in the plane", in each of which a small number of shades is used. According to Vitaly Manin, "from this color begins to sound more definite and intense, the emotional impact of it intensifies", as a result of which "the artist achieves the integrity of the impression".<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Манин|1976|p=53}}</ref>

==Sketches and variants==
The State Tretyakov Gallery holds a sketch sharing the title ''A Birch Grove'' (canvas, oil on canvas, 27 × 46.6 cm, 1879, inv. 11088), which had been in the possession of the artist [[Ilya Repin]] from 1879 and was given by him to the artist and collector [[Ilya Ostroukhov]] in 1903. The sketch was transferred from the Ostroukhov Museum to the Tretyakov Gallery in 1929.<ref name=":0" />

In the collection of the [[Russian Museum|State Russian Museum]] there are three sketches of the same title from 1879 — inventory No. Zh-1105 (oil on paper on cardboard, 19 × 29 cm), inventory No. Zh-1107 (canvas on cardboard, oil, 19.5 × 36.8 cm) and inventory No. Zh-1110 (sketch variant, paper on cardboard, oil, 21 × 33.5 cm). All three sketches came to the Russian Museum in 1930 from the [[Общество художников имени А. И. Куинджи|A. I. Kuindzhi Society of Artists]].<ref name=":19" /><ref name=":20" /><ref name=":21" />

Another sketch of the same title is in the collection of the State Art Museum of Nizhny Novgorod (canvas, oil, 19 × 36.4 cm, inv. Zh-1309).<ref name=":22" /><gallery mode="packed-overlay" caption="Sketches of the painting 'A Birch Grove' (1879)">

The second version of the painting ''A Birch Grove'' (canvas, oil, 165 × 115.5 cm),<ref name=":26">[https://www.sothebys.com/en/auctions/ecatalogue/2008/russian-art-n08428/lot.45.html 45: Arkhip Ivanovich Kuindzhi — A Birch Grove], 1881 (HTML). www.sothebys.com. Дата обращения: 8 June 2020. [https://web.archive.org/web/20200608055623/http://www.sothebys.com/en/auctions/ecatalogue/2008/russian-art-n08428/lot.45.html Archive]: 8 June 2020.</ref> presented at the exhibition in 1881, Kuindzhi wrote at the request of the industrialist and collector [[Pavel Pavlovich Demidov, 2nd Prince of San Donato|Pavel Demidov]], [[Princedom of San Donato|Prince of San Donato]], but for some reason their deal fell through. Then Kuindzhi tried to negotiate with the businessman Kozma Soldatyonkov, but he refused to buy the painting. In the end, the canvas was bought by the sugar manufacturer and collector Fyodor Tereshchenko for seven thousand rubles.<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Манин|1976|p=72}}</ref> For a long time the location of this variant was considered unknown, but then it was "found"{{Vague|date=May 2024}}<!-- Why the quotation marks? --> in a private collection in [[New York City|New York]]. In 2008 it was sold at a [[Sotheby's]] auction for 3.065 million [[United States dollar|dollars]].<ref name=":26" />

The third version of the painting ''A Birch Grove'' (1901, canvas, oil, 165.5 × 116 cm) in 1910 (after the author's death) became the property of the Artists' Society named after A.I. Kuindzhi. In 1918 it was sold to L.A. Sobotsinsky; later it was in the Leningrad collection of V. I. Pavlov. I. Pavlov. {{As of|2018}} this version was kept in the [[Belarusian National Arts Museum]] (inv. RZH-1443), where it came in 1954 from the funds of the Directorate of Art Exhibitions and Panoramas.<ref name=":24" />

==Reviews and critics==
[[File:Birch grove by Arkhip Kuindzhi at the Kuindzhi exhibition in Tretyakov gallery IMG 6386.jpg|left|thumb|The painting ''A Birch Grove'' at the 2018–2019 exhibition at the Tretyakov Gallery]]

Among the many landscapes exhibited at the 7th Travelling Exhibition, art critic Vladimir Stasov highlighted the works of Ivan Shishkin, Mikhail Klodt, and Arkhip Kuindzhi.<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Бенуа|1995|p=316}}</ref> Stasov wrote that Kuindzhi "possesses what few landscape painters have — an unusually poetic feeling and look. Noting that in Kuindzhi's work "everything always consists of one strongly felt and transmitted pictorial light effect, and everything else he has not finished, not studied, sacrificed", the critic recognized that "but this motif is always something poetic!" According to Stasov, ''A Birch Grove'' — a picture "with wonderfully illuminated trees and grass", but "very bad and incredible air". He noted that "there are many shortcomings everywhere, but what is good — it is good and original, like no one else, and takes notes of strong spectacular lighting, no one has not yet tried".<ref name=":17" />

The artist and critic [[Alexandre Benois|Alexander Benois]] in the book ''История русской живописи в XIX веке'' ("The History of Russian Painting in the 19th Century"), the first edition of which was published in 1902, recognized that A Birch Grove once so amazed the St. Petersburg public that many thought that to achieve the effect the author of the canvas resorted to "charlatan tricks", using additional lighting from the back or front. Benois noted that in ''A Birch Grove'' "we are now strongly disgusted by its crude form", "especially unpleasant is the ill-conceived "simplification", backstage construction, hitting the diorama ''[[trompe-l'œil]]''; at the same time, "it is already honorable that Kuindzhi felt the need for this simplification". Paying tribute to the artist's skill, Benois wrote that studying this painting "one is filled with great respect for its creator," who "made sure that every stroke 'meant' and sounded, that nothing was superfluous. According to Benois, in ''A Birch Grove'' is "remarkable for its bold, clear colors, not indifferent and technique".<ref>''Бенуа А. Н.'' История русской живописи в XIX веке. — М.: Республика, 1995. — 448 p. — P. 316. — {{ISBN|5-250-02524-2}}.</ref>

In an article dedicated to the 150th anniversary of Arkhip Kuindzhi's birth, art historian Vladimir Petrov wrote that ''A Birch Grove'' particularly brightly and directly embodies Kuindzhi's "sun worship". According to Petrov, on the basis of the everyday Central Russian motif, which includes a forest edge and flowing between white birch trees, the artist "created a hymn" pouring from the sky life-giving light. Petrov noted the "elevated and festive tone of the picture's imagery," which Kuindzhi achieved "with the help of bold generalization and intensity of contrasts, glowing in the sun and shaded color forms and zones, as well as rhythmic definition of the landscape solution, reminiscent of a kind of natural pattern and, to some extent, decoration ..."<ref>''Петров В. А.'' [http://kuinje.ru/petrov3.php Архип Иванович Куинджи // Архип Иванович Куинджи. 1842—1910. К 150-летию со дня рождения.] Каталог / В. А. Петров, Г. С. Чурак. — М.: Государственная Третьяковская галерея, 1992.</ref>

[[File:1991 CPA 6287.jpg|thumb|Painting ''A Birch Grove'' on a 1991 USSR postage stamp<ref>Почтовые марки СССР 1991 года (HTML). stamprus.ru. Дата обращения: 10 May 2020. [https://web.archive.org/web/20170630232737/http://stamprus.ru/marks/1991/ Archive]: 30 June 2017.</ref>]]

Art historian Faina Maltseva noted that ''A Birch Grove'' is "an innovative work", one of the best examples of realistic landscapes of the 1870s. At the same time, in her opinion, "some features of his painting raise legitimate objections among viewers". Maltseva attributes such features to "traits of conventionality" manifested "in a somewhat simplified color solution" — in particular, in order to achieve the greatest intensity of color, the artist had to sacrifice "some nuances in the characterization of individual objects," as well as "that which could give the landscape more variety of life".<ref name=":2" /> Nevertheless, according to Maltseva, in this work "Kuindzhi managed to create a real image filled with a great sound", and his skill "manifested itself here with particular force".<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Мальцева|2001|pp=52—53}}</ref>

The art historian Vitaly Manin wrote that in ''A Birch Grove'' Kuindzhi developed the search for a positive ideal that he had begun three years earlier in the painting ''[[Ukrainian Night]]''.<ref name=":18" /> One of Kuindzhi's most important innovations, according to Manin, was "a special construction of space and, in this connection, a new plastic understanding of volume".<ref name=":25" /> In addition, according to Manin, the "innovative essence" of the canvas could be attributed to the fact that "the artist succeeded in liberating the color, purifying it with light"; light is used as a "means of realistic transmission of nature" (from this point of view, ''A Birch Grove'' has much in common with some of [[Claude Monet]]'s early works, such as ''[[Woman in the Garden]]''). At the same time, Manin noted that the generalized painting of ''A Birch Grove'' creates a feeling of stasis, "gives the impression of numbness, of freezing".<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Манин|1976|p=54}}</ref> Nevertheless, according to Manin, "there was no picture in Russian landscape painting in which a bright sunny day was captured so joyfully and enlightened, in which the artist's peaceful feeling was so fully expressed, in which a bright sense of peace, uplifted mood received such a perfect embodiment".<ref name=":18" />

{{Short description|Altarpiece by Fra Angelico}} {{italic title}} {{Infobox artwork | title = Annunciation | other_language_1 = it | other_title_1 = Annunciazione | image = La Anunciación de Fra Angelico.jpg | artist = [[Fra Angelico]] | year = {{circa|1426}} | medium = [[Tempera|Tempera on]] [[Panel painting|panel]] | height_metric = 391 | width_metric = 493 | height_imperial = 154 | width_imperial = 194 | museum = [[Museo del Prado]] | city = [[Madrid]] }} The Prado '''''Annunciation''''' is an [[altarpiece]] painted by the [[Italian Renaissance]] painter Giovanni da Fiesole, known as [[Fra Angelico]], in the 1420s. It is one of his best-known works. Originally destined for the convent of the observant Dominicans of Fiesole, the painting is currently in the collection of the [[Museo del Prado]] in [[Madrid]]. It is one of three altarpieces by Fra Angelico representing the [[Annunciation]]; the other two being the Cortona ''[[Annunciation of Cortona|Annunciation]]'' and the ''[[Annunciation of San Giovanni Valdarno]]''. The sequence in which the three works were painted is not certain, but the general art historical consensus places the Prado version first. == History == The work was painted for a side altar in the [[Convent of San Domenico, Fiesole]], where Fra Angelico was a friar. For the same church he also contributed the [[Fiesole Altarpiece|main altarpiece]], showing the Virgin and Child Enthroned with Dominican saints (c. 1425) and the ''[[Coronation of the Virgin (Fra Angelico, Louvre)|Coronation of the Virgin]],'' now in the [[Louvre]] (c. 1424–1435) . The Annunciation remained at San Domenico until 1611 when it was sold to the King of Spain and taken to Madrid, where it became part of the royal collections of the [[Monarchy of Spain|Spanish monarchy]] before moving to Prado. == Description == [[File:Angelico,_dettaglio_vergine.JPG|thumb|The Virgin (detail)]] The scenes have a structure similar to the other two Annunciations but with some differences. As in the Annunciation of Cortona, the pictured surface is divided in three parts (the garden, the Angel's arch and the Virgin's arch), but the [[vanishing point]] is inside the home, as in the [[Annunciation of San Giovanni Valdarno|Annunciation of San Giovanni]], focusing the viewer's attention on the Annunciation. This scheme draws attention away from the figures of [[Adam]] and [[Eve]] expelled from [[Garden of Eden|Eden]], which in the Cortonese Annunciation are smaller but are near the vanishing point.[[Image:Fra Angelico 096.jpg|thumb|Detail: ''Adam and Eve hunted out of Paradise'' "walking on the roses of the garden of Mary"|left]] As in the other two works, they are moving in a flowered garden representing the virginity of Mary ("[[hortus conclusus]]"), inhabited by a multitude of plants and seedlings painted with great accuracy. Between the species with symbolic values, we can recognise the palm, representing the future martyrdom of Christ, and the red roses referring the blood of the [[Passion of Jesus|Passion]]. The presence of Adam and Eve evidences the cycle of the human damnation, recomposed with the deliverance in Christ made possible by the acceptance of Mary. From the high-left a ray of divine light illuminates, through the dove of [[Holy Spirit in Christianity|Holy Spirit]], the Virgin, who bends accepting her duty submissively. She's sitting on a seat covered with a rich drape acting as carpet, and she has on her knees an open book, symbol of the happening Scriptures. The Angel has a similar pose and vest to the work of San Giovanni, although his figure appears more static and the folds of the vest are more schematic, and may be the work of a collaborator. The scene is set under a Renaissance portico with the light arches stretched with wisdom on [[Perspective (graphical)|perspective]], which remember the architecture of [[Michelozzo]]. Light appears unified, unlike the pail of Cortona, and moves from left to right for all the element. == Predella == In the [[predella]] there are five scenes from Mary's life ( ''Birth and Marriage'', the ''Visitation'', the ''Adoration of the Magi'', ''Presentation at the temple'' and the ''dormition'') where the master had worked freely on the composition, less subjected to the iconographic tradition of the main scene. The ''Sposalizio'' presents the background of a Renaissance church with portico, while the visitation shows a sidelong lodge, represented with ability. This scene does not reach the vivid expression of fatigue on the woman who is going to the chime as in the predella of the ''[[Annunciation of Cortona]]''. The ''Adoration of the Magi'' instead is completely original and shows an innovative frontal iconography years before the revolution of [[Sandro Botticelli|Botticelli]] (''[[Adoration of the Magi (Botticelli, 1475)|Adoration of the Magi]]'' in the [[Uffizi]], 1475), enhanced by the complex perspective of the hut's ruins. Here can be noticed the distinct use of lights by Beato Angelico, who creates a pure and crystal illumination which models volumes, enhances the chromatic harmony and unifies the scenes. The following scene of the ''Presentation'' is more innovative, with the ambient placed inside a circular temple which seems projected through lens to the viewer, improving the scheme already used on the ''[[Presentation at the Temple (Gentile da Fabriano)|Presentation at the Temple]]'' by [[Gentile da Fabriano]]. The ''Dormition'' is the most traditional scene though the invention of the avvallamento between the background mountains can be considered innovative, because it creates a perspective channel to the holy way suspended by the Angels on the top.

'''''Chumaks Path in Mariupol''''' is an 1875 painting by Russian artist [[Arkhip Kuindzhi]] (1841/1842–1910). It is held in the collection of the [[State Tretyakov Gallery]] (inventory number 876). The painting measures 106 × 213 cm.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Chumaks path in Mariupol by Arkhip Kuindzhi {{!}} USEUM |url=https://www.useum.org/artwork/Chumaks-path-in-Mariupol-Arkhip-Kuindzhi |access-date=2025-05-12 |website=www.useum.org |language=en}}</ref>

==Description==
The painting is geographically linked to [[Mariupol]], where Kuindzhi was born and raised.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-03-07 |title=Чумацкий тракт в Мариуполе |url=http://www.artprojekt.ru/gallery/kuinji/kui04.html |access-date=2025-05-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307115111/http://www.artprojekt.ru/gallery/kuinji/kui04.html |archive-date=2016-03-07}}</ref> It depicts the southern steppes, familiar to the artist from his youth when traveling to [[Feodosia]]. The term "[[Chumak]]" historically referred to merchants and wagon drivers who traveled by oxen to the Black and Azov Seas for salt and fish, distributing these goods at markets and transporting various other commodities. [[Vsevolod Garshin]] wrote about the painting: "...Impassable mud, road, wet oxen, equally drenched Ukrainian peasants, and a wet dog diligently howling by the roadside about the dismal weather—all of it touches one's heart."

==History==
''Chumaks path in Mariupol'' was first exhibited at the 4th exhibition of the [[Peredvizhniki]] (the Society of Traveling Art Exhibitions) in 1875. Along with other realistic works by Kuindzhi from the early 1870s, such as ''[[Autumn Muddy Road (Kuindzhi painting)|Autumn Muddy Road]]'' (1872) and ''[[Forgotten Village (Kuindzhi painting)|Forgotten Village]]'' (1874), it received positive reviews from democratic publications. This marked the culmination of Kuindzhi’s close relationship with the Peredvizhniki, and he became a full member of the society in 1875.
[[Pavel Tretyakov]] purchased the painting directly from the 1875 exhibition. In 1878, Kuindzhi received the title of a first-degree [[Class artist]] for this work, along with paintings ''[[On the Island of Valaam]]'' (1873, Tretyakov Gallery), ''[[Ukrainian Night]]'' (1876, Tretyakov Gallery), and ''Steppe'' (1875, [[Yaroslavl Art Museum]]).<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-07-31 |title=Собрание картин, статьи, биография. Русский живопицец Архип Куинджи |url=http://kuinje.ru/voronova13.php |access-date=2025-05-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120731121839/http://kuinje.ru/voronova13.php |archive-date=2012-07-31}}</ref>

==Reception== 
Art historian [[Vladimir Petrov (art historian)|Vladimir Petrov]] compared the painting to ''[[Forgotten Village (Kuindzhi painting)|Forgotten Village]]'', noting: {{blockquote|Similar moods appear in ''Chumaks path in Mariupol'', where Kuindzhi depicted a caravan of Chumak wagons stretching across a brown steppe burnt by the summer sun and soaked by autumn rains. Details such as the Chumaks wrapped in wet sackcloth and a dog howling at the roadside are expressive. However, it would be incorrect, as some critics do, to see only a "protest sent into the void" in these gloomy works of Kuindzhi.}}
Writer [[Mikhail Nevedomsky]] described the painting: {{blockquote|The inclination towards Impressionism, towards generalized interpretation, appears decisively here. It is not individual wagons or Chumak figures, but the entire convoy, the general movement of this dark, living ribbon winding across the wide steppe, that occupies the artist. All details submerge into the general impression of gloomy steppe twilight.}}

'''''Hercules Fighting the Nemean Lion''''' is a work of 1634 by the Spanish painter [[Francisco de Zurbarán]]. It is conserved in the [[Museo del Prado]].

== Description ==
The painting depicts [[Heracles]] fighting the [[Nemean Lion]]. The Spanish art critic Soria suggests a comparison with a woodcut fashioned by [[Cornelis Cort]] after a work by [[Frans Floris]], based on the hero's position. The rocky setting was designed according to a woodcut by [[Barthel Beham]]: ''Fighting versus Centaur'' (1542).

It is one of series of 10 artworks on the [[Labours of Hercules]] commissioned by [[Philip IV of Spain]] for the decoration of the [[Hall of Realms]] in the [[Buen Retiro Palace]]. The series is now on display at the [[Museo del Prado]].

'''''Irises''''' is an oil painting by Dutch artist [[Vincent van Gogh]]. Painted in 1889, the work is a landscape with a cropped composition and is one of a [[Saint-Paul Asylum, Saint-Rémy (Van Gogh series)|series of several hundred paintings]] that van Gogh made at the [[Monastery of Saint-Paul de Mausole|Saint Paul-de-Mausole]] [[Lunatic asylum|asylum]] in [[Saint-Rémy-de-Provence]], France, in the last year before his death in 1890. It has been in the permanent collection of [[J. Paul Getty Museum|The Getty]] in Los Angeles, California since 1990.

The painting depicts vibrantly blooming irises with dynamic brushstrokes. The flowers are a mix of deep blues and violets, contrasting with lush green leaves, red-orange earth, and yellow flowers in the background. Van Gogh's characteristic [[impasto]] technique adds texture and movement within the painting, creating an energetic and expressive feeling. The overall cropped composition of Irises, includes broad areas of vivid color and monumental rippled irises overflowing the borders of the canvas which helps move the viewer's eye throughout the canvas.

== Background ==

=== Saint-Rémy ===
In May 1889, Van Gogh voluntarily entered the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum in nearby Saint-Rémy, where he painted around 150 canvases over the course of the next year. His initial confinement to the hospital grounds is reflected in his imagery, from depictions of its corridors to the irises and lilacs of its walled garden, visible from the window of the spare room allocated as his studio.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Paintings |first=Authors: Department of European |title=Vincent van Gogh (1853–1890) {{!}} Essay {{!}} The Metropolitan Museum of Art {{!}} Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History |url=https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/gogh/hd_gogh.htm |access-date=2024-10-12 |website=The Met’s Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History |language=en}}</ref> Vincent was restricted to the premises, where his only connection with nature was the enclosed garden and the view from his bedroom window. He visited the garden to find solace in painting, an early example of what is now called [[art therapy]]. In a letter to his brother [[Theo van Gogh (art dealer)|Theo]], Van Gogh mentioned that he had begun a painting of 'violet irises', a reference to ''Irises''. Van Gogh was optimistic about the restorative effects of painting in the hospital garden, writing: "I believe that all my faculties for work will come back to me quite quickly".<ref name=":0">Ultra-Violet: New Light on Van Gogh's Irises, published online in 2024, J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles, https://www.getty.edu/art/exhibitions/ultra-violet</ref>

Van Gogh started painting ''Irises'' within a month of his one-year stay at Saint-Paul-de-Mausole, in May 1889, working from nature in the hospital garden.<ref name=":1">Jennifer Helvey {{google books|LUZ-dHerY3sC|Irises: Vincent Van Gogh in the Garden|page=46}}</ref> Van Gogh himself regarded this painting as a study, and there are no known drawings for it.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Irises (The J. Paul Getty Museum Collection) |url=https://www.getty.edu/art/collection/object/103JNH |access-date=2024-10-12 |website=The J. Paul Getty Museum Collection |language=en}}</ref> ''Irises'' bears a direct trace of his work there: embedded in the paint is one of the pollen cones that fall in abundance from the umbrella pines in the garden.<ref name=":0" />

During his stay at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum, Van Gogh painted several depictions of irises. Another painting, ''Iris'', depicts a single iris among grasses. ''Iris'' must have been painted before ''Irises'', as it portrays just one mature flower and multiple developing buds, whereas ''Irises'' is filled with flowers, some of which have begun to wilt. [[Iris × germanica|Bearded irises]] bloom for around three weeks, with some variation depending on the temperature, so it can be inferred that the two paintings were separated by around ten days or so. Given that Vincent tells his brother Theo of his work on ''Irises'' in a letter written shortly after his arrival at the asylum, and given ''Iris's'' similarity in style and palette to four other nature studies usually dated to the end of his time in [[Arles]], it seems likely that ''Iris'' may be among the last things he painted before his admission to the asylum.<ref name=":1" />

After its completion in 1889, Van Gogh wrote to Theo to send him four rolls of canvases and seven studies, including ''Irises''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=789 (792, 600): To Theo van Gogh. Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, Sunday, 14 or Monday, 15 July 1889. - Vincent van Gogh Letters |url=https://vangoghletters.org/vg/letters/let789/letter.html |access-date=2024-10-12 |website=vangoghletters.org}}</ref>

=== Japanese influence ===
Van Gogh was a dedicated collector of Japanese prints.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Japanese Prints from Van Gogh's Collection |url=https://www.vangoghmuseum.nl/en/japanese-prints |access-date=2024-10-12 |website=Van Gogh Museum |language=en}}</ref> Like many European artists of his generation, Van Gogh immersed himself in the art of Japan. Japanese artists used large areas of colour in their compositions, often with a sharp diagonal. Japanese artists regularly focused in on detail in the foreground. Van Gogh associated irises with Japan, where the native species were highly prized and had a prominent place in art. Van Gogh adopted these elements in his paintings, but in his imagination he combined Japan and Provence. For him, both were exotic places that beckoned with a stronger sun, clearer skies and brighter colours.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Irises at the Getty |url=https://artsandculture.google.com/story/2QURLJeOYxo3ng |access-date=2024-10-12 |website=Google Arts & Culture |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Vincent van Gogh - Field with Irises near Arles |url=https://www.vangoghmuseum.nl/en/collection/s0037v1962 |access-date=2024-10-12 |website=Van Gogh Museum |language=en}}</ref>

The painting was most likely influenced by Japanese [[Ukiyo-e|ukiyo-e woodblock prints]] like many of his earlier works and those by other artists of the time.

=== Color scheme ===
A crucial part of Van Gogh's art was his ideas about [[color theory]]. Central to his understanding of color was the work of the French chemist [[Michel Eugène Chevreul|Michel-Eugène Chevreul]], whose law of simultaneous color contrast describes how our perception of a particular color is influenced by other colors in the vicinity. Chevreul postulated that each color has a specific complementary color. For example, red, yellow, and blue are complemented by green, purple, and orange. According to Chevreul, juxtaposing a primary color with its complementary secondary color{{em dash}}yellow next to violet, for example{{em dash}}intensifies both. Many artists found Chevreul's observations in [[Charles Blanc]]'s widely distributed G''rammaire des arts du dessin''. In this book, Blanc referred to the use of complementary colors by [[Eugène Delacroix]], a painter van Gogh greatly admired.<ref name=":0" />

=== Exhibition ===
''Irises'' was first exhibited at the [[Société des Artistes Indépendants]] in September 1889, along with ''[[Starry Night Over the Rhône]]''. Submitted by his brother Theo, he wrote to Vincent on 5 September 1889 to let him know the exhibition was open. Theo wrote, "Now I still have to tell you that the exhibition of the Indépendants is open, and that your two pictures are there, the 'Irises' and 'The Starlit Night'...They have to put it on the narrow wall of the room, and it strikes the eye from afar. It is a beautiful study full of air and life."<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Gogh |first=Vincent van |title=Van Gogh: a retrospective |last2=Stein |first2=Susan Alyson |date=1988 |publisher=Park Lane : Distributed by Crown |isbn=978-0-517-66122-2 |location=New York |pages=181}}</ref>

Theo also wrote about these two pieces to [[Wil van Gogh|Willemina]] 27 November 1889: "I submitted two paintings to the exhibition of the Indépendants that made a very good impression. A field of irises and the starry night, view of Arles with the street-lamps and the stars reflecting in the Rhône."<ref>{{Cite web |title=799 (800, T16): Theo van Gogh to Vincent van Gogh. Paris, Thursday, 5 September 1889. - Vincent van Gogh Letters |url=https://vangoghletters.org/vg/letters/let799/letter.html |access-date=2024-10-12 |website=vangoghletters.org}}</ref>

== Materials ==
The painting materials used in Van Gogh's artwork were analyzed by researchers and they used both "non-invasive methods and invasive methods" to analyze van Gogh's painting materials, according to Devi Ormond, Associate [[Paintings conservator|Paintings Conservator]] at the J. Paul Getty Museum. Non-invasive techniques helped identify "remnants of the red paint that we can’t see with the naked eye," while invasive methods, like creating cross-sections of the paint layers, revealed that beneath the blue top layer lies a faded violet. "As we go down deeper into the painting, you see this wonderful violet color," Ormond noted, explaining that it was originally created by mixing geranium lake red and blue—a combination that has since faded to reveal only the blue. 

The analysis also identified cobalt blue and ultramarine pigments, creating "many different shades and hues of violet" across the petals. Dr. Beth Harris observed that some areas now appearing as "muddy brown" were once "a brilliant orange," while Ormond pointed out that a "dirty-looking brown" in the flowers was initially a vivid red, showing the impact of color fading over time.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Smarthistory – Vincent van Gogh, Irises: the search for violet Getty Conversations |url=https://smarthistory.org/vincent-van-gogh-irises-the-search-for-violet-getty-conversations/ |access-date=2024-10-12 |website=smarthistory.org}}</ref>

== Interpretations ==
[[Félix Fénéon]], an early and avid spokesman for the [[Neo-Impressionism|Neo-Impressionists]] contributed his account of ''Irises'', which appeared in the [[Symbolism (movement)|symbolist]] review La Vogue in September 1889. Fénéon wrote "''Irises'' violently slash into long strips their violet petals on sword-like leaves."<ref name=":2" />

In a video by [[Smarthistory]], Dr. Scott Allan raises the question of how to categorise the artwork, reflecting on its intriguing viewpoint, which suggests that Van Gogh may have been sitting or kneeling. Allan notes that it doesn't fit the traditional definitions of [[Landscape painting|landscape]]{{em dash}}it lacks "the scale and the space and the view"{{em dash}}or the characteristics of a [[still life]]; it is not lifeless nor evokes "nature morte" or "dead nature". Instead, he emphasises that the irises depicted are "still rooted in the earth" and "intensely alive". This makes the subject a depiction of vibrant life rather than stillness, "It's a picture of moving life connected to the earth".<ref>Dr. Scott Allan, Dr. Steven Zucker and The J. Paul Getty Museum, "Vincent van Gogh, Irises Getty Conversations," in Smarthistory, March 28, 2022, accessed October 9, 2024, https://smarthistory.org/van-gogh-irises-getty-conversations/.</ref>

==Provenance==
The first owner was Julien "Père" Tanguy, a paint grinder and art dealer [[Portrait of Père Tanguy|whose portrait]] Van Gogh painted three times. In 1892 Tanguy sold ''Irises'' to [[art critic]] and [[Anarchism|anarchist]] [[Octave Mirbeau]] who was also one of van Gogh's first supporters.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.getty.edu/art/collection/objects/826/vincent-van-gogh-irises-dutch-1889/|publisher=J. P. Getty Museum|title=Irises}}</ref> Mirbeau paid 300 francs for it and later used it as a subject in his novel ''In the Sky''.

<!-- Editor's note: fill in the rest of the painting's ownership history -->
In 1987, it became the most expensive painting ever sold, setting a record which stood for two and a half years.<ref>Van Gogh's ''[[Portrait of Dr. Gachet]]'' sold for $82.5 million on May 15, 1990, at Christie's, New York</ref> Then it was sold for US$53.9 million to [[Alan Bond (businessman)|Alan Bond]], but Bond did not have enough money to pay for it.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.on-this-day.com/onthisday/thedays/alldays/nov11.htm |title=History for November 11 |publisher=On-This-Day.com |access-date=2012-11-17}}</ref> ''Irises'' was later re-sold in 1990 to the [[J. Paul Getty Museum]] in Los Angeles.<ref>{{cite news |last=Kimmelman |first=Michael |title=Getty Buys van Gogh 'Irises,' but Won't Tell Price |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=March 22, 1990 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/03/22/arts/getty-buys-van-gogh-irises-but-won-t-tell-price.html |access-date=March 20, 2011}}</ref> ''Irises'' is currently (as of 2022) thirty-first on the inflation-adjusted [[list of most expensive paintings]] ever sold and in 102nd place if the effects of inflation are ignored.

'''''Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan on 16 November 1581'''''{{efn|The work is variously referred to as ''Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan'', with or without the date, or ''Ivan the Terrible Kills His Son''.}} is a painting by Russian [[Realism (art movement)|realist]] artist [[Ilya Repin]] made between 1883 and 1885. It depicts the grief-stricken [[Tsars of Russia|Russian tsar]] [[Ivan the Terrible]] cradling his dying son, the [[Tsarevich]] [[Tsarevich Ivan Ivanovich of Russia|Ivan Ivanovich]], shortly after Ivan the Terrible had dealt a fatal blow to his son's head in a fit of anger. The painting portrays the anguish and remorse on the face of the elder Ivan and the shock and heartbreak of the dying Tsarevich, who sheds a tear at the unexpected betrayal and shock of having been killed at his father's hands.

Repin used [[Grigoriy Myasoyedov]], his friend and fellow artist, as the model for Ivan the Terrible, and writer [[Vsevolod Garshin]] for the Tsarevich. In 1885, upon completion of the oil-on-canvas work, Repin sold it to [[Pavel Tretyakov]] for display in his [[Tretyakov Gallery]] in Moscow.

It has been called one of Russia's most famous and controversial paintings, and is normally on display in the Tretyakov Gallery.

== Background and inspiration ==
{{multiple image
 | align = right
 | direction = vertical
 | width = 200
 | header =
 | image1 = Konstantin_Makovsky_Alexander_II_na_smertnom_odre_1881.jpg
 | caption1 = ''Emperor Alexander II on His Deathbed''. [[Konstantin Makovsky]].
 | image2 = Казнь_первомартовцев2.jpg
 | caption2 =  ''Execution of the Pervomartovtsy''.  A.A. Nesvetevich.
}}

Repin began working on the painting in Moscow.<ref name="RepinSite">{{cite web |title=История создания картины Репина 'Иван Грозный и сын его Иван' |url=http://ilya-repin.ru/ivan-grozny.php |website=Ilya Repin RU |access-date=18 November 2021 |language=ru}}</ref> A first overall sketch, with the character of the Tsar turned to his right, dates from 1882. The idea of the painting, according to Repin, is linked to his confrontation with the themes of violence, revenge and blood during the [[Assassination of Alexander II of Russia|political events of 1881]]; additional sources of inspiration were the music of [[Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov]] and the bullfights Repin had witnessed during a trip to Western Europe in 1883.

=== Political violence ===
On 13 March 1881 in [[Saint Petersburg]], the reformist Russian Tsar [[Alexander II of Russia|Alexander II]] was [[Assassination of Alexander II of Russia|assassinated]] by a bomb thrown by [[Ignacy Hryniewiecki]], a member of the revolutionary organization [[Narodnaya Volya]]. The bomb also seriously injured Hryniewiecki, who died a few hours later. Hryniewiecki's accomplices, the [[Pervomartovtsy]], were executed on 13 April 1881.{{sfn|Kel'ner|2015}}{{sfn|Yarmolinsky|2016|p=279}} Repin, who visited Saint Petersburg in mid-February 1881 for the opening of the [[Peredvizhniki|Wanderers]]' exhibition, was present when the tsar was killed. He returned there in April and attended the execution of the attack's perpetrators and their accomplices.<ref name="Lyaskovskaya">{{cite book |last1=Lyaskovskaya |first1=Olga |title=Илья Ефимович Репин |chapter=К истории создания картины И. Е. Репина «Иван Грозный и сын его Иван 16 ноября 1581 года» |url=http://artpoisk.info/article/k_istorii_sozdaniya_kartiny_i_e_repina_ivan_groznyy_i_syn_ego_ivan_16_noyabrya_1581_goda/ |access-date=18 November 2021 |location=Moscow |language=ru |date=1953 |trans-title=Ilya Yefimovich Repin}}</ref>

Repin's friend, poet [[Vasily Kamensky]], wrote in his memoirs Repin had told him "how he had witnessed the public execution of the Pervomartovtsy" ([[Andrei Zhelyabov|Zhelyabov]], [[Sophia Perovskaya|Perovskaya]], [[Nikolai Kibalchich|Kibalchich]], [[Timofey Mikhailov|Mikhailov]] and [[Nikolai Rysakov|Rysakov]]). "Ah, as it was nightmare times," – sighed Repin – "complex, appalling. I even remember each board on the breasts, with the inscription "regicide". I even remember Zhelyabov's gray pants, Perovskaya's black hat".<ref name="Lyaskovskaya" />

Several of Repin's next paintings; ''Refusal of confession'' ({{lang|ru|Отказ от исповеди}}; 1881), ''Arrest of a propagandist'' ({{lang|ru|Арест пропагандиста}}, 1882) and ''[[They Did Not Expect Him]]'' ({{lang|ru|Не ждали}}; 1884–1888); were devoted to the Pervomartovtsy. He also wrote several times in his memoirs about this period of his creations: "This year followed like a trace of blood, our feelings were bruised by the horrors of the contemporary world, it was frightening to confront it: it will end badly! ... We had to look for a way out at this key moment in history."<ref name="Nikonova">{{cite book |last1=Alexandrova |first1=Natalya |last2=Nikonova |first2=Natalya |last3=Vvedenskaya |first3=Elena |title=Герои и злодеи русской истории в искусстве XVIII — XX веков |date=2010 |location=Saint Petersburg |isbn=978-5-93332-355-6 |page=95 |language=ru |trans-title=Heroes and criminals in the history of Russian art from the 18th to the 20th century}}</ref><ref name="RepinSite2">{{cite web |title=Илья Репин. Галерея картин и рисунков художника - Иван Грозный и сын его Иван 16 ноября 1581 года, 1885 |url=http://ilya-repin.ru/master/repin4.php |website=Ilya Repin RU |language=ru |access-date=18 November 2021 |trans-title=Ilya Repin. Gallery of paintings and drawings of the artist – Ivan the Terrible and his son Ivan November 16, 1581, 1885}}</ref> For Repin, there was a link between the events of 1881 and the scene represented in ''Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan on 16 November 1581'' from exactly 300 years earlier, in which the Tsar is the murderer.<ref name="Lyaskovskaya" />

=== Music of Rimsky-Korsakov ===
Another inspiration for the painting was the symphonic suite ''[[Antar (Rimsky-Korsakov)|Antar]]'', which was composed by the Russian [[Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov]] and is composed of four movements; the opening movement, vengeance, power, and love.<ref name="Rakhmanova">{{cite web |last1=Rakhmanova |first1=Marina |title=Римский-Корсаков. 'Антар' (Antar, Op. 9) |url=http://www.belcanto.ru/rimsky_antar.html |website=Belcanto |access-date=18 November 2021 |trans-title=Rimsky-Korsakov. "Antar" (Antar, Op. 9)}}</ref>

The music of ''Antar''{{'s}} bloody second movement<ref name="Sedoy">{{cite web |last1=Vasiliev-Sedoy |first1=Victor |title=Репин. Реальность, парадоксы и мистика |url=https://proza.ru/2016/03/28/386 |website=Proza |access-date=18 November 2021 |trans-title=Repin. Reality, paradoxes and mysticism}}</ref> inspired Repin the most; he said in his memoirs:<ref name="Ionina">{{cite book |last1=Nadezhda |first1=Ionina |title=Сто великих картин |date=2000 |publisher=Вече |location=Moscow |isbn=978-5-7838-0579-0 |language=ru |trans-title=Hundred great paintings}}</ref><ref name="RepinSite" />
{{blockquote|In Moscow in 1881, while I was listening to a new piece by Rimsky-Korsakov, ''Vengeance'' ("''Месть''"). This sound wave took possession of me, and I thought, that I could not embody the state of the soul I had known under the influence of this music in a painting. I then remembered Tsar Ivan.<ref name="Ionina" />}}

=== Trip to Europe ===
Repin's painting is also striking because of its representation of blood, which is seeping from the Tsarevich's temple and remains on the floor in a puddle after his father has picked him up. According to Repin's memoirs, he was influenced by his 1883 trip to Europe, where he witnessed bullfights:
{{blockquote|Misfortune, death, murder and blood make up a hole that draws you into it with force. At the same time, there are so many bloody paintings in all the exhibitions. And I, probably overtaken by all this bloodiness, on my return home, started the bloody scene of Ivan the Terrible with his son. And this painting had a great success.<ref name="RepinSite2" />}}

== Creation ==
According to Repin, the design and painting of the canvas were a lengthy process:

{{blockquote|I painted in tears, I was tortured, I tormented myself, I corrected again and again what I had painted, I hid it, in a sickly disappointment, no longer believing in my strength, I erased what I had painted. I had already erased, and I was attacking the canvas again. Every minute was terrible to me. I was disappointed with this painting, I hid it. And it made the same impression on my friends. But something pushed me towards it, and again I was working on it.<ref name="Ionina" />}}

The painting depicts one of the rooms of the {{ill|Chambers of the Romanov Boyars|ru|Палаты Романовых}} from the 17th century while the accessories, throne, mirror, and [[kaftan]] were painted at the [[Kremlin Armoury]]. The chest is part of the collections of the [[Rumyantsev Museum]].<ref name="RepinSite" />

Most of Repin's work involved the choice of models; he sought the faces he needed from acquaintances and passers-by. The models for Ivan the Terrible were the painter [[Grigoriy Myasoyedov]] and the composer {{ill|Pavel Blaramberg|ru|Бларамберг, Павел Иванович}}, while the landscape painter {{ill|Vladimir Menk|ru|Менк, Владимир Карлович}} and writer [[Vsevolod Garshin]] modelled for Tsarevich Ivan Ivanovich.<ref name="RepinSite2" /> When he was asked about choosing Garshin, Repin replied:

{{blockquote|There is a predestination in Garshin's face that struck me. He has the face of a man irreparably condemned to perish. This is what was needed for my Tsarevich.<ref name="Prorokova">{{cite book |last1=Prorokova |first1=Sophia |title=Репин |date=1960 |publisher=Молодая гвардия |location=Moscow |page=209 |language=ru |trans-title=Repin}}</ref>}}

According to Polish-American art historian [[Elizabeth Kridl Valkenier]], the incorporation of Garshin's face completes and allows her to be fully satisfied with the painting.<ref name="met">{{cite journal |last1=Valkenier |first1=Elizabeth |author1-link=Elizabeth Kridl Valkenier |title=The Writer as Artist's Model: Repin's Portrait of Garshin |journal=Metropolitan Museum Journal |date=1993 |volume=28 |pages=211–212 |doi=10.2307/1512927 |jstor=1512927 |s2cid=155366014 |url=https://www.metmuseum.org/pubs/journals/1/pdf/1512927.pdf.bannered.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191002123234/https://www.metmuseum.org/pubs/journals/1/pdf/1512927.pdf.bannered.pdf |access-date=18 November 2021|archive-date=2 October 2019 }}</ref>

== Analysis ==
=== Moment represented ===
{{multiple image
| direction = vertical
| width = 220
| image1   = Ivan the Terrible killing his son (sketch, 1882, GRM).jpg
| image2    = Répine Ivan le Terrible et son fils Ivan esquisse sur toile 1882-1899.jpg
| image3    = Répine Ivan le Terrible et son fils Ivan principale version 1883 - 1885.jpg
| footer = From top to bottom: {{ulist|pencil sketch (1882 – 20.7 × 27.1 cm);|oil sketch (1883, 1899 – 22.2 × 36 cm);|Final version (1884–1888).}}
}}
Although the painting is sometimes called ''Ivan the Terrible Kills His Son'', Repin did not paint the moment at which the Tsar hits the Tsarevich. The work does not represent violence but its resolution.<ref name="met" /> Ivan the Terrible holds his son. His eyes "bulging with horror, despair and madness",<ref name="arthive">{{cite web |last1=Esaoulova |first1=Alena |title=Илья Ефимович Репин – «Иван Грозный и его сын Иван 16 ноября 1581 года» |url=https://arthive.com/ilyarepin/works/294983~Ivan_the_terrible_and_his_son_Ivan_on_16_November_1581 |website=Art Hive |access-date=18 November 2021 |archive-date=23 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240523071733/https://arthive.com/ilyarepin/works/294983~Ivan_the_terrible_and_his_son_Ivan_on_16_November_1581 |url-status=dead }}</ref> he embraces him by the waist. Tsarevich Ivan, weeping, gently waves his hand.<ref name="met" />

Two modifications to the preliminary sketches show the distance established by the painter with the altercation; the sceptre with which the Tsar strikes his son's temple is in his hand in the first sketches while in the final painting, it is on the floor in front of them.<ref name="arthive" /><ref name="met" /> The bloodstain where the Tsarevich's head rests on the floor, which is very visible in the oil sketch Repin made in 1883, and which he kept and resumed later, is erased in the shadows of the final painting. Ivan Ivanovich's dress no longer has a long bloodstain. The represented moment becomes one of remorse, forgiveness and love.<ref name="met" /> The painting also shows, in its centre, the reality and the irreversibility of the tsar's act: the blood flows from his son's temple and the attempt Ivan the Terrible makes to contain it with his left hand is hopeless.<ref name="arthive" />

=== Description and composition ===
The painting's {{Convert|199.5|×|254|cm|ftin|abbr=on|0}} canvas is one of Repin's largest works; its dimensions are comparable to those of the ''[[Barge Haulers on the Volga]]'' and the ''[[Religious Procession in Kursk Governorate]]''.<ref name="Churak">{{cite book |last1=Churak |first1=Galinina |title=Илья Репин |date=2014 |publisher=[[Tretyakov Gallery]] |isbn=978-5-89480-032-5 |page=35 |oclc=49657097 |language=ru |trans-title=Ilya Repin}}</ref>

The two characters are crisscrossed with each other in the centre of the painting. They are depicted in a twilight<ref name="Churak" /> and stand out from both the foreground of the canvas and the darker background.<ref name="arthive" /><ref name="Fetzer">{{cite journal |last1=Fetzer |first1=Leland |title=Art and Assassination: Garshin's 'Nadezhda Nikolaevna' |journal=The Russian Review |date=1975 |volume=34 |issue=1 |pages=55–65 |jstor=127759 |doi=10.2307/127759 }}</ref> The gesture with which Ivan the Terrible hugs and supports his son's waist is reminiscent of the paintings ''[[The Return of the Prodigal Son (Rembrandt)|The Return of the Prodigal Son]]'' and ''[[David and Jonathan (Rembrandt)|David and Jonathan]]'' by Dutch painter [[Rembrandt]],  which Repin studied and admired since his formative years, and are housed in the [[Hermitage Museum]].<ref name="met" /><ref name="Lyaskovskaya" />

The construction of the painting is based on objects and pieces of furniture that are distributed around the characters: the crumpled red carpets on the floor, the Tsarevich's boots, the sceptre, the throne that was overturned during the argument, one of the ornamental balls that sparkles at the level of the son's eyes, and his cushion.<ref name="arthive" /> Behind the figures, other pieces of furniture, such as the stove, the mirror of the Armor Museum and the chest of the Rumyantsev Palace, are less discernible. The back wall of the room is partly covered with a red-and-black diamond pattern. At the top left is a narrow bay.<ref name="RepinSite" />

=== Colours and material ===
[[File:Tsarevich's boots by Repin.jpg|180px|alt=Pair of crisscrossed green boots on a red background.|thumb|Sketch of the Tsarevich's boots (1883).]]

Repin wrote he refused "the acrobatics of the brush and painting for the sake of painting"<ref name="Chukovsky">{{cite book |last1=Chukovsky |first1=Korney |author1-link=Korney Chukovsky |title=Илья Репин |date=1969 |location=Moscow |page=59 |language=ru |trans-title=Ilya Repin}}</ref> and that "the beauty, the touch or the virtuosity of the brush" was not the only important things because he had always pursued "the essential: the body, as a body".<ref>{{cite book |last=Repin |first=Ilya |author-link=Ilya Repin |date=1937 |title=Далёкое близкое |trans-title=Distant close |url=https://www.prlib.ru/item/1272678 |location=Moscow |publisher=Захаров |page=351 |isbn=978-5-8159-0204-6 |language=ru}}</ref> ''Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan'' is "painted with such a diversity of craftsmanship and with such a rich palette of dark chords" that it is, according to Russian painter and art critic [[Ivan Kramskoi]], an "authentic orchestra".<ref name="Churak" /> An "intense red"<ref name="ikleiner">{{cite web |last1=Nadezhda |first1=Ionina |title=Репин И. Иван Грозный убивает своего сына |url=https://www.ikleiner.ru/lib/picture/picture-0050.shtml |website=Ikleiner |access-date=18 November 2021 |language=ru |trans-title=Ivan the Terrible kills his son}}</ref> or "blood red",<ref name="nearyou">{{cite web |author1=Н.Д. Моргунова-Рудницкая |title=И.E. Репин – Иван Грозный и сын его Иван 16 ноября 1581 года |url=http://nearyou.ru/repin/t85ioan.html |website=NearYou |access-date=18 November 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180630151404/http://nearyou.ru/repin/t85ioan.html |archive-date=30 June 2018 |language=ru}}</ref> and "thick and saturated crimson red" predominates.<ref name="Churak" /> It is painted with pure colour, with no additions, and then reworked by the painter with an extraordinary diversity of shades.<ref name="ikleiner" />

The scarlet red of the blood flowing from the wound on the Tsarevich's temple stands out, as do the reflections on the folds of his kaftan, and finally the dark-red puddle of blood on the red carpet, and this tension of colours resonates with the tragedy depicted on the canvas.<ref name="ikleiner" /> In the centre, the magnificence of the Tsarevich's kaftan contrasts with the darkness of Ivan the Terrible's black coat.<ref name="nearyou" /> Repin breaks this combination of blood red, pink and dark-brown tones with the complementary tones of the green of the Tsarevich's boots and the deep-blue of his velvet trousers.<ref name="nearyou" /> White light, "cold and weak", which penetrates through a narrow bay, attenuates this tension of colours and further reinforces the dramatic tension of the scene.<ref name="ikleiner" />

=== Symbolic scope ===
[[File:Иллюстрация к рассказу «Четыре дня». (Рисунок худ. Дубровского.).jpg|thumb|Illustration by painter Doubrovsky from Vsevolod Garchine's short story "{{ill|Four Days (short story)|ru|Четыре дня|lt=Four Days}}".<br>The writer's first work, it exhibits the interior monologue of a soldier wounded and left for dead on the battlefield for four days, face to face with the corpse of a Turkish soldier he has just killed. His deep empathy for all beings is already there.]]

For Repin and his contemporaries, the painting's first symbolic function is to express the existence of violence and moral rejection, which must be the object. According to [[Ivan Kramskoi]]; "it seems that a human being, after having carefully looked at this painting, even if only once, will be forever protected from the wild beast he has, as they say, in him".<ref name="RepinSite2" />

The representation of the aftermath of the father's altercation with his son is a historical episode and illustrates a person's "eternal" capacity to physically harm their neighbour. The painting can be understood as a pictorial parable of the commandment "[[Thou shalt not kill]]".<ref name="RepinSite2" /><ref name="Churak" />

The picture also seemed to approach a more-particularly religious inspiration, showing "Christian love and forgiveness" can repair crime, even [[filicide]].<ref name="met" /> The tsarevich's gesture and face are "almost like that of an icon", and the tear that runs down the wing of his nose seems to depict forgiveness.<ref name="arthive" /> The similarity of the gesture of Ivan the Terrible's right arm with those of the figures in the two Rembrandt paintings also aligns with this position.<ref name="met" />

In the interpretation of the work, the personality of the writer [[Vsevolod Garshin]] provides additional details. In this period, Repin used Garshin as a model in several other paintings, including ''{{ill|Portrait (Repin)|fr|Portrait de Vsevolod Garchine|lt=Portrait}}'' (1884) and the large painting ''They Did Not Expect Him'', in which Garshin poses for the main character. Work on ''They Did Not Expect Him'' began in 1884 and ended the year of Garshin's suicide in 1888.<ref name="met" />

Repin appreciated Vsevolod Garshin, whom he considered an "incarnation of the divine" during their friendship and after his death. He wrote "his pensive eyes, often mixed with tears provoked by some injustice, his humble and delicate attitude, his angelic personality, with the purity of a dove, were those of a God". Repin's painting refers to Garshin's physical features, his personality and his deeply peaceful thought.<ref name="met" />

=== A representation of power ===
[[File:Nikolay Ge 064.jpg|upright=1.3|200px|thumb|[[Nikolai Ge]] – Sketch for ''Peter the Great interrogates Tsarevich Alexis in Peterhof'' (1871).|alt=Pencil drawing.]]

The political significance of the painting cannot be eluded because of the reactions to which it was immediately the subject. Repin combined Ivan the Terrible's killing of his son with the [[Assassination of Alexander II of Russia|assassination of Alexander II]]. Repin and Russian art critics did not expand upon this point;<ref name="Lyaskovskaya" /> however French critics did. According to [[Alain Besançon]], the tsarevich's murder by the tsar is a central scene of the Russian myth, which Repin was the first to represent: the history of Russia would be built on the sacrifice of sons killed by their fathers.<ref name="Marion">{{cite web |last1=Poirson-Dechon |first1=Marion |title=Du sacrifice d'Isaac au tsarévitch immolé |url=http://www.tramayfondo.com/actividades/viii-congreso/ponencias/pon08_8congreso_infancia-y-violencia.pdf |website=Tramay Fondo |access-date=18 November 2021 |language=fr |date=2016 |trans-title=From the sacrifice of Isaac to the slain tsarevich}}</ref>

Pierre Gonneau supports a converging position, stressing this sacrificial vision refers "to the symbolic roots of the monarchy because the sacrificed tsarevich finds himself in a position to embody the forces opposing the authority of the tsar".<ref name="Pierre" /> It makes a link with the trial of [[Alexei Petrovich, Tsarevich of Russia|Tsarevich Alexis]], son of [[Peter the Great]], and his death as a result of torture. This other conflict between a father and his son is the theme of [[Nikolai Ge]]'s 1871 painting ''[[Peter the Great Interrogating the Tsarevich Alexei Petrovich at Peterhof|Peter the Great Interrogating the Tsarevich Alexei at Peterhof]]''.<ref name="Pierre">{{cite web |last1=Gonneau |first1=Pierre |title=Comment s'est forgée l'image d'Ivan le Terrible |url=https://lejournal.cnrs.fr/billets/comment-sest-forgee-limage-divan-le-terrible |website=CRNS Journal |access-date=18 November 2021 |language=fr |trans-title=How the image of Ivan the Terrible was forged |date=2014}}</ref>

=== 1909 version ===
In 1909, on a commission from the industrialist and collector {{ill|Stepan Ryabushinsky|ru|Рябушинский, Степан Павлович}}, Repin painted a second version of ''Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan'', which he called ''Filicide'' ({{lang|ru|Сыноубийца}}). It is on display at Voronezh Museum of Fine Arts.<ref name="Tretyakov" /> The second version  was painted 25 years later than the first. In this version, Repin added a female character in the background and unveiled more colours than in the original painting, taking it in a more "luxuriant" direction, while Tsar Ivan's face is collapsed in grief.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Gnezdilova |first1=Olga |title=Как Илья Репин изменил картину об Иване Грозном через 25 лет после ее создания |url=http://umbra.media/specproject/kak-ilya-repin-izmenil-kartinu-ob-ivane-groznom-cherez-25-let-posle-ee-sozdaniya/ |website=UMBRA |date=5 August 2017 |access-date=18 November 2021 |language=ru |trans-title=How Ilya Repin changed the painting about Ivan the Terrible 25 years after its creation}}</ref>

== Reception and initial censorship ==
In 1885, ''Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan'' was shown for the first time to Repin's painter friends, among whom were [[Ivan Kramskoi]], [[Ivan Shishkin]], [[Nikolai Yaroshenko]] and [[Pavel Brullov]]. According to Repin, his hosts were stunned and silent for a long time, waiting to see what Kramskoi would say:

{{blockquote|text=I was seized with a feeling of complete appreciation for Repin. There it is, the thing, what a level of talent ... And how it's painted, my God, how it's painted! ... And what is this murder, carried out by a wild beast and a psychopath? ... A father hits his son with his sceptre in the temple? One moment ... He utters a cry of terror ... He grabs him, he sits him on the ground, he raises him ... He presses one of his hands on the wound in the temple (and blood gushes out of the cracks between the fingers) ... and as he bawls ... It's an animal, howling with fear ... the very spot that the son has marked with his temple ... Really, this scene is drowning us in half-light and a kind of natural tragic.|author=[[Ivan Kramskoi]]<ref name="tanais.info">{{cite web |title=Илья Репин. Иван Грозный и сын его Иван 16 ноября 1581 |url=http://www.tanais.info/art/repin74more.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131017001803/http://www.tanais.info/art/repin74more.html |archive-date=17 October 2013 |website=Tanais |access-date=18 November 2021 |language=ru |trans-title=Ilya Repin. Ivan the Terrible and his son Ivan on 16 November 1581}}</ref>}}

The very conservative Attorney General of the [[Most Holy Synod]] [[Konstantin Pobedonostsev]] told [[Alexander III of Russia|Alexander III]] of his "repulsion" and perplexity about the painting,<ref name="Pierre" /> which did not please the Tsar and his entourage, and on 1 April 1885, viewings of the painting were forbidden. It was the first painting to be censored in the Russian Empire,<ref name="tanais.info" /> and [[Pavel Tretyakov]], who bought it, was told "not to expose it, and more generally not to allow it to be brought to the attention of the public by any other means". The ban was lifted on 11 July 1885 after the intervention of the painter [[Alexey Bogolyubov]].<ref name="RepinSite2" /><ref name="tanais.info" />

== Vandalism and controversies ==

 | align = right
 | direction = horizontal
 | width = 160
 | image1 = Ivan the Terrible & son - destroyed.jpg
 | caption1 = Damage to the painting from the 1913 attack
 | image2 = Ivan the Terrible killing his son 2018 vandalism damage.jpg
