On 16 January 1913, ''Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan on 16 November 1581'' was slashed three times with a knife by {{ill|Abram Balachov|ru|Балашов, Абрам Абрамович}}, a 29-year-old [[iconoclast]] and [[Old Believer]]. The curator of the Tretyakov gallery {{ill|Georgy Khruslov|ru|Хруслов, Георгий Моисеевич}}, learning of the vandalism of the canvas, committed suicide by throwing himself under a train.<ref name="scepsis.net">{{cite web |last1=Troitsky |first1=Nikolay |title=Культура: Искусство // Россия в XIX веке: Курс лекций |url=https://scepsis.net/library/id_1552.html#_ftnref12 |website=Scepsis |access-date=18 November 2021 |language=ru |trans-title=Culture: Art // Russia in the 19th century: Course of Lectures}}</ref> The painting was restored almost to its original state with the help of Repin; Balachov was admitted to the {{ill|Moscow Psychiatric Hospital No. 1|ru|Психиатрическая клиническая больница № 1 имени Н. А. Алексеева}}.<ref name="tanais.info" /><ref>{{cite journal|last=Karaseva|first=Alexandra Timofeevna|title=Мистификация вокруг картины Иван Грозный и сын его Иван 16 ноября 1581 года|trans-title=The hoax surrounding the painting Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan on November 16, 1581|journal=Business and Design Review|issue=1 (29)|year=2023|pages=79–85|url=https://archive.obe.ru/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/10.-Karaseva.pdf|language=ru|access-date=10 October 2026}}</ref>

Some [[Russian nationalist]]s continue to protest the painting's exhibition because they believe it was painted as part of a foreign smear campaign and that the scene depicted is inaccurate.<ref name="theguardian">{{cite web |last1=Bodner |first1=Matthew |title=Ivan the Terrible painting 'seriously damaged' in pole attack |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2018/may/27/famous-russian-painting-of-ivan-the-terrible-seriously-damaged-in-pole-attack |website=[[The Guardian]] |access-date=18 November 2021 |date=27 May 2018}}</ref>

In October 2013, a group of Orthodox historians and activists, led by Vassili Boiko-Veliki, an apologist and supporter of the canonization of Tsar Ivan, addressed the [[Ministry of Culture of the Russian Federation|Minister of Culture of the Russian Federation]] [[Vladimir Medinsky]] to ask him to remove the canvas from the Tretyakov Gallery on the grounds it offends the patriotic feelings of Russians.<ref name="echo.msk">{{cite web |title=Православные активисты требуют убрать из Третьяковки картьяковки картину Репина |url=https://echo.msk.ru/news/1169794-echo.html |website=echo.msk.ru |access-date=18 November 2021 |language=ru |trans-title=Orthodox activists demand that Repin's painting be removed from the Tretyakov Gallery}}</ref><ref name="theguardian" /> The director of the Tretyakov Gallery Irina Lebedeva formally opposed the request.<ref name="theguardian" />

In May 2018, the canvas was again attacked in the Tretyakov Gallery by a drunken visitor who broke its protective glass with a metal bar. The painting suffered serious damage; it was pierced in three places in the central part of the work, which depicts the figure of the tsarevich. The gallery said the frame was also badly damaged but that "by a happy coincidence" the most precious elements of the painting, the depiction of the figures' faces and hands, were not damaged. According to some Russian media, the vandal said he had attacked the painting because he thought the depiction was inaccurate.<ref name="theguardian" /> The attacker was imprisoned for two-and-a-half years.<ref name="rferl">{{cite web |title=Russian Sentenced For Vandalizing Iconic Painting Of Ivan The Terrible |url=https://www.rferl.org/a/russian-sentenced-to-2-1-2-years-for-vandalizing-iconic-painting-of-ivan-the-terrible/29912342.html |website=[[Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty]] |access-date=26 November 2021 |date=30 April 2019}}</ref> Following extensive restoration works, the painting was placed on display on 16 December 2024.<ref>{{cite web |title=Repin Painting Returns to Moscow's Tretyakov Gallery Nearly 7 Years After Vandal Attack |url=https://www.themoscowtimes.com/2024/12/16/repin-painting-returns-to-moscows-tretyakov-gallery-nearly-7-years-after-vandal-attack-a87343 |website=[[The Moscow Times]] |access-date=16 December 2024 |date=16 December 2024}}</ref>

== Legacy ==
''Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan'' remains one of Russia's most famous paintings, and the most psychologically intense of Repin's works.<ref name="nytimes">{{cite web |title='Ivan the Terrible' Painting Damaged in Russia in Vodka-Fueled Attack |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/05/27/world/europe/ivan-the-terrible-painting-attack.html |website=[[New York Times]] |access-date=26 November 2021 |date=27 May 2018}}</ref> The work appears briefly in the third episode of the 2019 [[HBO]] miniseries ''[[Chernobyl (miniseries)|Chernobyl]]''.<ref name="Chernobyl">{{cite web |title=Chernobyl |url=https://www.artpapers.org/chernobyl/ |date=17 July 2019 |website=Art Papers |access-date=18 November 2021}}</ref>

== Subject of the painting and historiography ==
The Tsarevich Ivan's death had grave consequences for Russia, since it left no competent heir to the throne. After the Tsar's death in 1584, his unprepared son [[Feodor I]] succeeded him with [[Boris Godunov]] as ''de facto'' ruler. After Feodor's death, Russia entered a period of political uncertainty, famine and war known as the [[Time of Troubles]].<ref>"Britannica - Fyodor I". ''Encyclopedia Britannica''.</ref>

The details of the Tsarevich's death are unknown and controversial. The Tsarevich died in 1581 in the [[Alexandrov Kremlin]], the residence of Tsar [[Ivan the Terrible]] from 1564 to 1581, and the centre of his [[oprichnina]] and ''de facto'' capital of the [[Tsardom of Russia]].<ref>{{cite book | last1=Perrie | first1=Maureen | last2=Pavlov | first2=Andrei | title=Ivan the Terrible | publisher=Taylor and Francis | publication-place=Hoboken | date=2014 | isbn=978-1-317-89468-1 | oclc=884014235}}</ref>

=== In contemporary Russian chronicles and sources ===
In a letter addressed to [[Nikita Romanovich|Nikita Zakharin]] and [[Vasily and Andrey Shchelkalov#Andrey Yakovlevich Shchelkalov|Andrey Shchelkalov]] in 1581, Ivan the Terrible wrote; "[he] cannot go to Moscow because of [his] son's illness" without identifying the illness.<ref name="Likhachyov">{{cite book |language=ru |last=Likhachyov |first=Nikolay |author-link=Nikolay Likhachyov |title = Дело о приезде в Москву А. Поссевино |trans-title =The case of A. Possevino's arrival in Moscow |page = 58 |place = Saint Petersburg |date = 1903 |isbn = |url=https://viewer.rusneb.ru/ru/rsl01003714039?page=58&rotate=0&theme=white }}</ref> Several contemporary Russian chronicles mention the Tsarevich's death without providing any details.<ref name="MoscowChronicle">{{cite encyclopedia |title=Московский летописец |encyclopedia=[[Complete Collection of Russian Chronicles]] |accessdate=18 November 2021 |year=1978 |volume=34 |location=Moscow |language=russian |trans-title=Moscow chronicle |url=http://www.russiancity.ru/books/b60.htm |page=228}}</ref> According to the Piskarevsk Chronicle, the death occurred at midnight. None of these chronicles suggest the death of Ivan Ivanovich was violent.<ref name="Piskarevsk">{{cite encyclopedia |title=Пискаревский летописец |encyclopedia=[[Complete Collection of Russian Chronicles]] |accessdate=18 November 2021 |year=1978 |volume=34 |location=Moscow |url=http://www.russiancity.ru/books/b61.htm |page=195 |language=ru |trans-title=Piskarevsky chronicle}}</ref> Other sources provide a more-detailed version of the death, saying the Tsarevich was mortally wounded by his father during an argument. One of these sources, the {{ill|Mazurin chronicle|ru|Мазуринский летописец}}, reports the following:<ref name="Mazurin">{{cite encyclopedia |title=Мазуринский летописец |encyclopedia=[[Complete Collection of Russian Chronicles]] |accessdate=18 November 2021 |year=1978 |volume=31 |location=Moscow |url=http://psrl.csu.ru/toms/Tom_31.shtml |page=142 |language=ru |trans-title=Mazurin chronicle}}</ref>

{{blockquote|In the summer of 1581, it was from the Sovereign Emperor and Grand Prince Ivan Vassilievitch, that his son, his greatness Prince Tsarevich Ivan Ivanovich, shining with wise meaning and grace and separated from the branch of life by a blade, received evil, and from this evil, he died.<ref name="Mazurin" />}}

The sources indicate the event took place on 14 November 1581 and that the Tsarevich would have died on 19 November, but the dates reported vary. The diary of the ''[[Dyak (clerk)|dyak]]'' (clerk) {{ill|Ivan Timofeev|ru|Семёнов, Иван Тимофеевич}} says; "some say (of the Tsarevich) that his life was extinguished because of blows by the hands of his father, after trying to prevent him from committing an ugly act".<ref name="vremen">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mELRAAAAMAAJ |title=Временник Ивана Тимофеева |publisher=Publishing house of the USSR Academy of Sciences |author=Timofeev Ivan |year=1951 |trans-title=Annals of Ivan Timofeev |page=182}}</ref>

=== Foreign testimonies ===
Contemporaneous foreign sources are more eloquent; [[Jacques Margeret]], a French mercenary captain in service in Russia, wrote; "there is a rumour that he (the tsar) killed the eldest (son) with his own hand, which wasn't the case, because, although he struck him with the end of the rod and he was wounded by a blow, he did not die from this, but some time later, on a pilgrimage journey".<ref name="Margeret">{{cite book |url=https://www.prlib.ru/item/450931 |title=Состояние Российской империи и Великого княжества Московского |year=1986 |location=Leningrad |trans-title=State of the Russian State and the Grand Duchy of Moscow in 1606 |language=ru |last1=Jacques |first1=Margeret | last2=Nikolaevich |first2=Ilya |author1-link=Jacques Margeret |page=232 }}</ref>

Another version is reported by the papal diplomat [[Antonio Possevino]]. According to him, in November 1581 in the Alexandrov Kremlin, Ivan the Terrible found his daughter-in-law Helen lying on a bench in undergarments.{{efn|The female dress of this period usually consisted of two undergarments, the bottom, the shirt, and the top, the dress. The shirt was a garment for domestic use, and it was considered very improper to appear to strangers in it, especially in front of men.<ref name="Zabelin">{{cite book |title=Домашний быт русских цариц в XVI-XVII столетиях |author=Zabelin Ivan |author1-link=Ivan Zabelin |year=1901 |location=Moscow |isbn=978-5-373-07405-6 |trans-title=Household life of Russian queens in the XVI-XVII centuries |language=ru |page=515 }}</ref>}}

{{blockquote|text=The third wife of Ivan's son was laying on a bench, dressed in underwear. She was pregnant and didn't expect anyone to visit her. However, the Grand Prince of Moscow (Ivan the Terrible) paid her an unexpected visit. She immediately stood up to meet him, but it was already impossible to calm him down. He hit her in the face, and then beat her with his staff, punching her so hard that she lost her child the next night.

His son Ivan then ran to his father and asked him not to beat his wife, but this only made his father angrier. The Prince started hitting his son with his staff, which resulted in a very serious wound in the head. Before that, in anger at his father, the son hotly reproached him in the following words:

"You imprisoned my first wife in a convent for no reason, you did the same with my second wife, and now you are beating up the third in order to kill the child she carries in her womb." Having injured his son, the father immediately indulged in deep grief and immediately summoned doctors and Andrei Shchelkalov and Nikita Romanovich from Moscow to have everything at hand. On the fifth day, the son died and was transferred to Moscow.
|author=Antonio Possevino
|source=''Historical writings about Russia in the 16th century''<ref name="Possevino">{{cite book |last1=Possevino |first1=Antonio |author1-link=Antonio Possevino |title=Исторические сочинения о России XVI в |date=1983 |publisher=Moscow University Publishing House |location=Moscow |url=http://krotov.info/acts/16/possevino/041.html |access-date=18 November 2021 |language=ru |trans-title=Historical writings about Russia in the 16th century}}</ref>}}

=== Stories by Russian historians ===
18th-century Russian historian [[Nikolay Karamzin]] also believed the Tsarevich died because of his father but under different circumstances.<ref name="Karamzin">{{cite encyclopedia |title=Продолжение царстования Иоанна Грозного. Г. 1577–1582 |encyclopedia=History of the Russian State |author=Karamzin, Nikolay | volume=9 |author-link=Nikolay Karamzin |language=ru |trans-title=Continuation of the reign of Ivan the Terrible. 1577–1582 |chapter=9}}</ref>
{{blockquote
|text=He (Ivan the Terrible) put his hand on him (Tsarevich). [[Boris Godunov]] wanted to come to his aid but the Tsar inflicted several wounds to him with the point of his [[sceptre]] and struck the Tsarevich with it on the head. He then fell to the ground, spilling his blood. The father's fury disappeared. Paling with fear, trembling, in complete shock, he exclaimed "I killed my son" and he threw himself down to kiss him; pouring out the blood flowing from a deep wound, he wept, sobbed, called for the doctors. He implored the mercy of God and the forgiveness of his son.
|author=Nikolay Karamzin}}

Repin relied on Karamzin's story to paint ''Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan on 16 November 1581'', one of the most-striking paintings of his [[chrestomathy]].<ref name="Tretyakov">{{cite web |last=Yudenkova |first=Tatyana |title='I love variety...' Ilya Repin's Indefatigable Novelty Across Time and Genre |url=https://www.tretyakovgallerymagazine.com/articles/1-2019-62/i-love-variety-ilya-repin-indefatigable-novelty-across-time-and-genre |website=[[Tretyakov Gallery]] |access-date=18 November 2021 |date=2019 }}</ref> Russian imperial historian [[Mikhail Shcherbatov]], who studied the different versions of Ivan Ivanovich's death, considers Possevino's version the most plausible<ref name="Shcherbatov">{{cite encyclopedia |encyclopedia=История Российская с древнейших времен |accessdate=18 November 2021 | author=Shcherbatov, Mikhail |year=1789 |volume=5 |chapter-url=https://www.runivers.ru/upload/iblock/3eb/sherbatov%20-%20istoriya5-3.pdf |chapter=3 |pages=120–126 |author-link=Mikhail Shcherbatov }}</ref> and the Russian imperial historian [[Vasily Klyuchevsky]] called it the only reliable version.<ref name="Klyuchevsky">{{cite book |last1=Klyuchevsky |first1=Vasily |author1-link=Vasily Klyuchevsky |title=Курс русской истории |language=ru |trans-title=A History of Russia |location=Saint Petersburg}}</ref>

'''''March''''' is a [[landscape painting]] by the Russian artist [[Isaac Levitan|Isaaс Levitan]] (1860–1900), created in 1895. It is now in the [[Tretyakov Gallery|State Tretyakov Gallery]] in [[Moscow]] (Inventory 1489) and measures 60 × 75 cm<ref name=":0">{{Harvard citation text|State Tretyakov Gallery catalogue, vol. 4, book 1|2001|p=362}}</ref> (or 61 × 76 cm according to other sources).<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Левитан Исаак Ильич — Март |url=https://www.tretyakovgallery.ru/collection/mart/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150925094946/http://www.tretyakovgallery.ru/ru/collection/_show/image/_id/293 |archive-date=25 September 2015 |access-date=13 May 2019 |publisher=Государственная Третьяковская галерея — www.tretyakovgallery.ru}}</ref> Levitan painted the picture in March 1895 while living in the Gorka estate, in the [[Vyshnevolotsky Uyezd]] of [[Tver Governorate]].<ref name=":0" />

The painting ''March'' was exhibited at the 24th exhibition of the [[Peredvizhniki|Society for Travelling Art Exhibitions]] (Peredvizhniki)<ref name=":8">{{Harvard citation text|Товарищество передвижных художественных выставок|1987|Ref=Товарищество передвижных художественных выставок|p=485}}</ref> in February 1896 in [[Saint Petersburg]]. It was later moved to Moscow in March of the same year.<ref name=":9">{{Harvard citation text|Рогинская|1989|p=419}}</ref> ''March'' was exhibited at the [[All-Russia Exhibition 1896|All-Russia industrial and art exhibition 1896]] in [[Nizhny Novgorod]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":11">{{Harvard citation text|Левитан|1966|p=54}}</ref> In the same year, [[Pavel Tretyakov]] purchased the painting from the author.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":12">{{Harvard citation text|Чижмак|2010|p=69}}</ref>

''March'' is considered to be one of Levitan's 'life-affirming, cheerful works' from 1895 to 1897. This group also includes ''Golden Autumn'' (1895), ''[[Fresh Wind. Volga]]'' (1895), and ''Spring. Big Water'' (1897), among others.<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Прытков|1960|p=9}}</ref><ref>{{Harvard citation text|Фёдоров-Давыдов|1975|p=533}}</ref> The painting ''March'' is widely regarded as one of Levitan's most famous and vivid landscape paintings.<ref name=":13">{{Harvard citation text|Иовлева|2010|p=5}}</ref> It also demonstrates the influence of [[Impressionism]] on the artist's oeuvre.<ref name=":17">{{Cite web |title=Левитан Исаак Ильич |url=https://www.tretyakovgallery.ru/collection/?author=levitan |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160708210518/http://www.tretyakovgallery.ru/ru/collection/_show/author/_id/104 |archive-date=8 July 2016 |access-date=13 May 2019 |publisher=Государственная Третьяковская галерея, www.tretyakovgallery.ru}}</ref>

Artist [[Vasily Baksheev]] praised the painting, considering it not only one of Levitan's best works, but also one of the best works of the Russian school of painting.<ref name=":18">{{Harvard citation text|Левитан|1956|p=146}}</ref> According to art historian [[Aleksei Fedorov-Davydov|Alexei Fedorov-Davydov]], Levitan's painting ''March'' was a 'discovery in Russian landscape painting', combining a pictorial depiction of snow, spring sky, and trees. This motif later became a popular theme for many Russian landscape painters of the 20th century, including [[Igor Grabar]] and [[Konstantin Yuon]].<ref name=":19">{{Harvard citation text|Фёдоров-Давыдов|1975|p=536}}</ref> According to art historian Faina Maltseva, ''March'' is a 'inspired work in a major tone' that presents 'a whole and internally complete image, preserving at the same time all the immediacy and freshness of first impressions.'<ref name=":20">{{Harvard citation text|Мальцева|2002|p=31}}</ref>

== History ==

=== Background and creation ===
In 1894–1895, Levitan resided for several months at the Gorka estate, which is situated one and a half kilometres from the village of Ostrovno. The estate is now part of the [[Udomelsky District]] of the [[Tver Oblast]], but at that time, it was part of the [[Vyshnevolotsky Uyezd]] of the [[Tver Governorate]]. The estate, located on the southern shore of Lake Ostrovno, was owned by [[Privy Councillor (Russia)|Privy Councillor]] Ivan Nikolayevich Turchaninov. His wife, Anna Nikolayevna, often spent time there with their daughters Varvara, Sofya, and Anna.<ref name=":16">{{Harvard citation text|Ионина|2006}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Исторические усадьбы России — Усадьбы Тверской области — Усадьба Горка |url=http://hist-usadba.narod.ru/links5-31.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20121225043255/http://hist-usadba.narod.ru/links5-31.html |archive-date=25 December 2012 |access-date=30 March 2015 |publisher=hist-usadba.narod.ru}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Антон Павлович Чехов — Имение Горка |url=http://litmap.tverlib.ru/chehov/gorka.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130211033739/http://litmap.tvercult.ru/chehov/gorka.html |archive-date=11 February 2013 |access-date=16 November 2019 |publisher=Литературная карта Тверского края, litmap.tvercult.ru}}</ref><ref group="Note">Anna Nikolayevna Turchaninova, née Makarova (25 May 1856 – 24 November 1930, Paris), was four years older than Levitan. Her daughters were Varvara Ivanovna (around 1875 – 1925), Sofia Ivanovna (1877 – around 1825) and Anna Ivanovna (2 December 1880, [[Vyshny Volochyok|Vyshny Volochok]] – 1964, Leningrad).</ref>{{Sfn|Подушков|2014|pp=116—126}}{{Sfn|Подушков|2018|p=51}} The manor's main building is a two-storey house with a [[mezzanine]], painted in a yellowish hue. It is depicted in Levitan's painting ''March'' and his earlier [[pastel]] ''Autumn. The Manor'' (1894),<ref name=":2" /> currently stored in the [[Vrubel Museum of Fine Arts|Omsk Regional Museum of Fine Arts named after M.A. Vrubel]].<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Каталог ООМИИ|2012|p=108}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Левитан Исаак Ильич — Осень. Усадьба, 1894 |url=http://www.art-catalog.ru/picture.php?id_picture=63 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402112051/http://www.art-catalog.ru/picture.php?id_picture=63 |archive-date=2 April 2015 |access-date=31 March 2015 |publisher=www.art-catalog.ru}}</ref><ref>{{Harvard citation text|Королёва|2009|pp=29, 48}}</ref>
[[File:Левитан Осень. Усадьба.jpg|left|thumb|230x230px|[[Isaac Levitan]]. ''Autumn. The Manor'' (pastel, 1894, Omsk Regional Museum of Fine Arts named after M.A. Vrubel)]]
In the early 1870s, the Turchaninovs acquired the land near Lake Ostrovno and replaced the old one-storey house left by the previous owners with a two-storey house. Additionally, they owned one of the lake islands, which featured a gazebo and benches. In the documents of the Statistical Committee of the Tver Province, there is the following description of the estate: 'The estate 'Gorka' on the southern peninsula of Lake Ostrovnoe. The place is beautiful. To the south behind the manor there is a pine forest, directly overlooking the lake, its islands, the eastern shore with a [[pogost]] and the manor of the village 'Ostrovno', and the western steep shore covered with birch forest. To the east and west of the house there are birch groves, cleared, with made paths... The 'Gorka' estate is perfect as a holiday home. Dry, sandy land, healthy pine air and a beautiful forest, a garden and a wonderful view of the lake with its green islands, a white church and a tall old tavern of the village 'Ostrovno.'<ref name=":3">{{Harvard citation text|Подушков|2009}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Harvard citation text|Подушков|2014|pp=116–126}}</ref>
[[File:Левитан Весна. Последний снег.jpg|thumb|230x230px|Isaac Levitan. ''Spring. The Last Snow'' (sketch, 1895, [[Russian Museum|State Russian Museum]])]]
Levitan first met Anna Nikolaevna Turchaninova in the summer of 1894 in Ostrovno. He was a guest at the Ushakov estate<ref group="Note">The Ostrovno estate was owned by Ekaterina Nikolaevna Ushakova (née Seslavina, 1821–1910) and her children Varvara Vladimirovna (1849 – about 1919), Sofia Vladimirovna (1851 – about 1919) and Nikolay Vladimirovich (1859–1917). Levitan and [[Sofia Kuvshinnikova|Kuvshinnikova]] stayed at the Ushakovs' estate during the summer of 1893 while the artist was working on the painting ''[[Over Eternal Peace]]'', and returned in 1894.</ref>{{Sfn|Подушков|2009}}{{Sfn|Чижмак|2010|p=67}} with his companion, the artist [[Sofia Kuvshinnikova]]. Levitan and Turchaninova had a romantic relationship, which resulted in a quarrel and the end of Levitan's relationship with Kuvshinnikova. Following this, Levitan relocated to the Gorka estate where he resided during August and September 1894. He returned to the estate in the early spring of the following year.<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Чижмак|2010|p=67}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Сергеев |first=Илья |date=24 August 2012 |title=Гений русского пейзажа — Исаак Левитан и тверские страницы его биографии |url=https://vedtver.ru/news/society/geniy-russkogo-peyzazha/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304074252/http://www.vedtver.ru/news/8623 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |access-date=13 May 2019 |publisher=«Тверские ведомости» — www.vedtver.ru}}</ref> As there were no appropriate rooms at the estate, an artist's workshop was constructed. The two-storey building was situated on the shore of the lake, at the confluence of the Syezha River (the same one depicted in Levitan's later painting ''[[Golden Autumn (painting)|Golden Autumn]]'').<ref name=":14">{{Harvard citation text|Подушков|2018|p=51}}</ref><ref name=":2" /> It was humorously referred to as a 'synagogue'.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Harvard citation text|Подушков|2014|p=51}}</ref>

In March 1895, Levitan created the painting ''March''. The artwork was painted entirely from nature, without preliminary [[Study (art)|studies]], in a few sessions. This may have been the first time Levitan created a canvas directly [[en plein air]].<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Фёдоров-Давыдов|1966|p=202}}</ref> The youngest daughter of the Turchaninovs, Anya (known as Lyulyu within the family), who was 14 years old at the time, witnessed the artist's work on the painting ''March''.<ref name=":3" /> She assisted the artist in carrying a box of paints, listened to his stories about the beauty of nature, and observed the creation of a future masterpiece.<ref name=":5">{{Harvard citation text|Пророкова|1960|p=160}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Harvard citation text|Кац|1983|p=|loc=chapter 2}}</ref> In later publications, the youngest daughter of the Turchaninovs was occasionally mistakenly referred to as Julia, likely due to its similarity to the name Lyulyu.<ref name=":6" />
[[File:Korovin Winter 1894.jpg|left|thumb|230x230px|[[Konstantin Korovin]]. ''Winter'' (1894, [[Tretyakov Gallery|State Tretyakov Gallery]])]]
The writer Sofia Prorokova, author of a biography of Levitan published in 1960, recounted her meeting with Anna Ivanovna Turchaninova<ref group="Note">Sofia Prorokova's memoirs provide a detailed account of how she located Anna Ivanovna Turchaninova (Lyulyu). While visiting Lake Ostrovno, local residents informed her that E A. Zvorykina, the sister of Anna Ivanovna's first husband, resided in Leningrad. Prorokova obtained Zvorykina's address through the address bureau, which ultimately led her to Anna Ivanovna's residence.</ref>{{Sfn|Пророкова|1989|p=29}} (first married Zvorykina, second married Kolokoltsova):<ref name=":6" /><ref>{{Harvard citation text|Колокольцов|2000}}</ref> 'Years would pass, Anya would grow up, and this sunny spring would remain a vivid memory of her distant youth. We are sitting in her Leningrad flat, talking to an elderly woman whose dark eyes retain both cunning and fire. Memories of Levitan have become like a family heirloom. She is one of the Turchaninova family's living witnesses to how the artist's best paintings were created in Gorka.' Prorokova quoted Anna Ivanovna's words: '''March'' was painted in front of me.'<ref name=":5" />

During the spring of 1895, Levitan also painted ''Spring. The Last Snow'', which is now held in a private collection in Moscow.<ref name=":7">{{Harvard citation text|State Russian Museum catalogue, vol. 6|2016|p=104}}</ref> The painting was previously in the collection of Moscow patron of the arts Vladimir Shmarovin. A sketch of the same name is held in the [[Russian Museum|State Russian Museum]] (25.5 × 33.3 cm, canvas, oil, inv. Zh-4261).<ref>{{Harvard citation text|State Russian Museum catalogue|1980|p=178}}</ref><ref name=":7" /> In 1895, Levitan created several paintings while working on the Gorka estate, including ''Golden Autumn'' (now in the [[Tretyakov Gallery|State Tretyakov Gallery]]) and ''Nenuphar'' (now in the Astrakhan Picture Gallery named after P. M. Dogadin).<ref>{{Harvard citation text|State Tretyakov Gallery catalogue, vol. 4, book 1|2001|pp=363–364}}</ref>

The painting ''March'' is sometimes said to be preceded by the 1894 landscape ''Winter'' by Russian impressionist painter [[Konstantin Korovin]] (now in the [[Tretyakov Gallery|State Tretyakov Gallery]]). ''Winter'' also depicts a horse and sleigh standing near a village house. However, unlike Levitan's sunny spring canvas, Korovin's painting portrays a gloomy winter day.<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Алленов|1989|p=407}}</ref><ref>{{Harvard citation text|Киселёв|2001|p=15}}</ref>

=== 24th traveling exhibition and subsequent events ===
Together with nine other works by [[Isaac Levitan|Levitan]], including ''Golden Autumn'', ''[[Fresh Wind. Volga]]'', ''Spring. The Last Snow'', ''Ferns in a Forest'', ''Twilight'', and ''Nenuphar'', the canvas ''March'' was exhibited at the 24th exhibition of the [[Peredvizhniki|Society for Travelling Art Exhibitions]] ('Peredvizhniki')<ref name=":8" /> in [[Saint Petersburg]] on 11 February 1896.<ref group="Note">The [[Julian calendar]] ("old style") is used to date events that took place in the [[Russian Empire]].</ref> The exhibition then moved to [[Moscow]] in March of the same year. The exhibition was split between two locations: the Saint Petersburg exhibit was held in the building of the [[Imperial Society for the Encouragement of the Arts|Society for the Encouragement of the Arts]], while the Moscow exhibit was held in the premises of the [[Moscow School of Painting, Sculpture and Architecture]].<ref name=":9" /> Levitan's canvases, which were quite diverse, received mixed reviews from critics.<ref name=":10">{{Harvard citation text|Фёдоров-Давыдов|1966|p=227}}</ref> In particular, in the note 'The Exhibition of Peredvizhniki', published in the '[[Vsemirnaya Illyustratsiya|Vsemirnaya Illustratsiya]]' (Vol. 55, No. 1413 for 1896), Vladimir Chuiko praised Levitan for his choice of subjects and his peculiar way of painting, noting that 'almost all his paintings (10 in number) attract attention, with the exception of two: ''March'' and ''Spring'', which are too rough and harsh in tone.' According to Chuiko, 'the shortcomings noted in Mr Levitan's manner will disappear, we hope, in the near future, when his talent finally strengthens.'<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Фёдоров-Давыдов|1966|pp=378–379}}</ref><ref>{{Harvard citation text|Чуйко|1896|p=231}}</ref> Nevertheless, the majority of the reviews about Levitan's work were positive, indicating 'recognition of the artist's talent, the originality of his work and his radiant individuality.'<ref name=":10" />

The painting ''March'' was also exhibited at the [[All-Russia Exhibition 1896|All-Russia industrial and art exhibition]], which opened on 28 May 1896 in [[Nizhny Novgorod]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":11" /> Levitan himself visited the exhibition, where a total of eighteen of his paintings were displayed.<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Круглов|2001|p=16}}</ref><ref>{{Harvard citation text|Захаренкова|2010|pp=219–220}}</ref> In addition to works from the travelling exhibition, a number of Levitan's works from the late 1880s and early 1890s were presented in Nizhny Novgorod. This was the first wide retrospective display of the artist's work.<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Захаренкова|2010|p=220}}</ref> In 1896, [[Pavel Tretyakov]] purchased the paintings ''March'' and ''Golden Autumn'' from the author.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":12" /> The 24th travelling exhibition continued its journey to other cities of the [[Russian Empire]] in autumn and winter, visiting [[Kharkiv]] (October–November), [[Kyiv]] (December–January) and [[Tula, Russia|Tula]] (January–February).<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Товарищество передвижных художественных выставок|1987|p=523|Ref=Товарищество передвижных художественных выставок}}</ref> The exhibition catalogue issued in Kharkiv described the paintings as 'property of the Moscow City Gallery of brothers P. and [[Sergei Tretyakov (arts patron)|S]]. Tretyakovs'.
[[File:March by Isaac Levitan in the State Tretyakov Gallery IMG 6312.jpg|thumb|230x230px|The painting ''March'' in the Levitan Hall<ref group="Note">Hall No. 37 of the main building in Lavrushinsky Lane</ref> of the [[Tretyakov Gallery|State Tretyakov Gallery]]]]
The Gorka estate did not survive the revolutionary upheavals of the early 20th century. Levitan's house workshop, where he worked in the mid-1890s, burned down in 1904.<ref name=":2" /> Ivan Nikolayevich Turchaninov deceased in 1910,<ref name=":14" /> and in 1914, the estate was sold to Aggey Aggeyevich Markov, a [[second guild merchant]].<ref name=":2" /> Before the sale, Anna Ivanovna Turchaninova (Lyulyu) visited Gorka. The artist [[Vitold Byalynitsky-Birulya]], who was in the area, described the meeting. In particular, he recognised the place in Levitan's painting: "As we approached the black porch of the house, my heart trembled at the image that suddenly appeared before me. ...This place was familiar to me. Only, everything was in winter dress, and the barrel was on a sledge. That ''March'' was before my eyes".<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Подушков|2018|p=161}}</ref> Apparently, the artist [[Stanislav Zhukovsky]] was also present. In another description of the same meeting, Byalynitsky-Birulya wrote: "We walked past the black porch, where the view falls on a magnificent [[Pine barrens|barren]], which everyone knows from Levitan's painting ''March''. We all involuntarily cried out in joy: "Look, this is what ''March'' was painted from!"<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Горелов|1982|p=32}}</ref> In June 1923, a few years after the [[October Revolution|revolution]], the mansion was destroyed by fire, the cause suspected to be arson.<ref name=":2" />

The painting ''March'' was exhibited at several exhibitions, including [[Isaac Levitan|Levitan's]] personal exhibition in 1938 at the [[Tretyakov Gallery|State Tretyakov Gallery]], and the jubilee exhibition in 1960–1961 in Moscow, [[Leningrad]], and [[Kyiv]]. However, it only participated in the Moscow part of the exposition.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Harvard citation text|State Tretyakov Gallery catalogue, vol. 4, book 1|2001|p=463}}</ref> The painting was exhibited in [[London]] in 1959 as part of an exhibition of Russian and Soviet artists.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":15">{{Harvard citation text|State Tretyakov Gallery catalogue, vol. 4, book 1|2001|p=471}}</ref> It was also featured in the 1971–1972 exhibitions 'Peredvizhniki in the State Tretyakov Gallery' (Moscow) and 'Landscape Painting of the Peredvizhniki' (Kyiv, Leningrad, [[Minsk]], Moscow) to commemorate the centenary of the [[Peredvizhniki|Society for Travelling Art Exhibitions]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":15" /> It was exhibited at the anniversary exhibitions for the 150th anniversary of Levitan's birth, held in the Benois Building of the [[Russian Museum|State Russian Museum]] (April–July 2010)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Исаак Левитан (1860—1900). К 150-летию со дня рождения |url=https://rusmuseum.ru/benois-wing/exhibitions/isaac-levitan-1860-1900-to-mark-the-150th-anniversary-since-the-birth-of/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210123112557/https://rusmuseum.ru/benois-wing/exhibitions/isaac-levitan-1860-1900-to-mark-the-150th-anniversary-since-the-birth-of/ |archive-date=23 January 2021 |access-date=18 July 2021 |publisher=Государственный Русский музей — rusmuseum.ru}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Лузина |first=О. |date=30 April 2010 |title=Левитан в Русском музее: Чем ёлка лучше пальмы |url=https://www.fontanka.ru/2010/04/30/070/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180402042523/http://www.fontanka.ru/2010/04/30/070/ |archive-date=2 April 2018 |access-date=18 August 2021 |publisher=Фонтанка.ру — www.fontanka.ru}}</ref> and in the New Tretyakovka on [[Krymsky Val]] (October 2010 – March 2011).<ref name=":13" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Махонин |first=А. |date=18 October 2010 |title=В Третьяковской галерее юбилейная выставка Исаака Левитана |url=https://www.vedomosti.ru/lifestyle/articles/2010/10/18/unylaya_pora_ochej |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151003035548/http://www.vedomosti.ru/lifestyle/articles/2010/10/18/unylaya_pora_ochej |archive-date=3 October 2015 |access-date=6 August 2021 |publisher=Ведомости — www.vedomosti.ru}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Исаак Левитан. К 150-летию со дня рождения |url=http://www.museum.ru/N41169 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170504041321/http://www.museum.ru/N41169 |archive-date=4 May 2017 |access-date=6 August 2021 |publisher=Музеи России — www.museum.ru}}</ref> In September 2017, the painting ''March'' was displayed at the 'exhibition of one masterpiece' at the Primorsky State Art Gallery in [[Vladivostok]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Исаак Левитан. "Март". Выставка одного шедевра в Приморской картинной галерее |url=http://www.museum.ru/N67406 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210806111811/http://www.museum.ru/N67406 |archive-date=6 August 2021 |access-date=6 August 2021 |publisher=Музеи России — www.museum.ru}}</ref>

During Levitan's jubilee exhibition in Moscow in 2010–2011, an [[opinion poll]] was conducted to determine visitors' preferences. The results of the poll showed that ''March'' was the third most popular work of the artist, behind only the large-format canvases ''[[At the Pool]]'' (1892, State Tretyakov Gallery) and ''[[Over Eternal Peace]]'' (1894, State Tretyakov Gallery).<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Петрунина|2012|p=616}}</ref> The painting ''March'' is currently exhibited in the Levitan Hall (Room No. 37) of the main building of the [[Tretyakov Gallery]] in Lavrushinsky Lane.<ref name=":1" />

== Description ==
The painting by Levitan depicts the backyards of the Gorka estate, with the yellow wall of the main house visible on the right side of the painting.<ref name=":2" /> The scene is set on a sunny day in March, with melting snow, trees, and a country road leading up to the porch. A horse with a sleigh stands still, basking in the sun, on the country road approaching the porch.<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Петров|1992|p=93}}</ref> The horse, named Dianka, is positioned in the centre of the painting and is an integral part of the landscape.<ref name=":16" /><ref>{{Harvard citation text|Пророкова|1960|p=159}}</ref> At the same time, according to the literary critic Andrei Turkov, "the house did not enter the composition of the picture at a favourable angle – a part of the wall with poorly visible windows, a porch with a half-thawed roof, a drainpipe, recently fallen boards from the windows, boarded up for the winter".<ref name=":21">{{Harvard citation text|Турков|1974|p=90}}</ref> According to art historian [[Mikhail Alpatov]], the wall of the house with planks that extend deep into the canvas, and the thawed country road "draw the viewer into the painting, help him to enter it mentally."<ref name=":22">{{Harvard citation text|Алпатов|1945|p=25}}</ref>
[[File:RooksBackOfSavrasov.jpg|left|thumb|235x235px|[[Alexei Savrasov]]. ''[[The Rooks Have Returned]]''  (1871, [[Tretyakov Gallery|State Tretyakov Gallery]])]]
The painting's main motif depicts the contrast between winter and spring, sunlight and snow. This is highlighted by the colour contrast between the dark [[Pine|pine trees]] in the background and the light, sunlit trunks of the deciduous trees (while some authors refer to them as [[Common aspen|aspens]]{{Sfn|Прытков|1960|p=9}}{{Sfn|Петров|1992|p=93}} or [[Birch|birch trees]],{{Sfn|Турков|1974|p=90}} others do not specify which trees are depicted on the canvas){{Sfn|Алпатов|1945|p=25}}{{Sfn|Лужецкая|1965|p=260}}{{Sfn|Фёдоров-Давыдов|1966|pp=201—202}}{{Sfn|Лясковская|1966|p=125}}{{Sfn|Мальцева|2002|p=31}} in front of them, which appear to be reaching for the spring sun with their branches.<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Фёдоров-Давыдов|1966|pp=201–202}}</ref> A [[birdhouse]] is positioned unusually high on one of the trees, giving the impression that it is attached to a branch that is too thin.<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Петров|1992|pp=93–94}}</ref> The light-coloured trunks of the trees on either side of the canvas appear to lean towards each other. The scene conveys a sense of slight motion, with the deciduous trees, pines, ajar door partly covered with shadows, and [[Window shutter|shutter]] lying next to the porch all appearing to move.<ref name=":23">{{Harvard citation text|Фёдоров-Давыдов|1975|p=202}}</ref> The horizontal edge of the snow-covered field, extending to the distant coniferous trees, divides the painting into two roughly equal parts and "brings a note of tranquillity to it."<ref name=":22"/> The shades of snow, the blue shadows of the trees and the blue sky create a very picturesque image. This subject is repeated many times in the landscapes of other Russian artists.<ref name=":19" />

The three main colours that define the colour scheme of the canvas are yellow, blue and green, with white added in places. Yellow is found not only on the wall of the house and on the ajar door, but also on the tops of the trees and in shades of horse hair. Most of the blue is present in the depiction of the cloudless spring sky; this blue is combined with the blue used to paint the shadows of the trees, as well as with the greyish blue tones of the snow in the background. The [[Crown (botany)|crowns]] of the conifers are painted in shades of green from light to dark. The most complex combinations of primary colours are found in the paintings of the deciduous trees and the rutted road.<ref name=":23" /> Despite the presence of many subtle shades and reflexes, the colour palette of the painting is "extremely sonorous, much more sonorous than in any of Levitan's previous paintings". The primary colours do not only have intensity but also definition, which is most evident in the colouring of the yellow wall of the house, the blue sky and the green pines.<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Фёдоров-Давыдов|1975|p=204}}</ref> When analysing the colours used to paint ''March'', art historian Tatyana Kovalenskaya observed that they coincided with the shades of painting of Yaroslavl [[fresco]]es listed by Levitan himself: “whitewash, [[ochre]], blue, something like green earth.”<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Коваленская|1983|p=146}}</ref>

Although close in subject to [[Alexei Savrasov]]'s famous canvas ''[[The Rooks Have Returned]]'' (1871, [[State Tretyakov Gallery]]), the painting ''March'' differs significantly from it in painting technique.<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Пилипенко|1994|p=74}}</ref> It is a vivid example of the so-called ‘Levitan’s landscape’ – a ‘landscape of mood’, in which the artist, despite depicting the ‘jubilant state of nature,’ managed to preserve the lyrical shade of experience and sadness in the painting.<ref name=":13" /><ref>{{Harvard citation text|Ильина|2000|p=222}}</ref> Unlike Savrasov's ''Rooks'', where the narrative character dominates and the landscape is largely interpreted through genre means, in ''March'' there is "a desire for a direct sensual and visual representation of natural phenomena",<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Фёдоров-Давыдов|1966|p=206}}</ref> with "an intimate perception of the everyday environment conveyed in the feeling of warm air melting the heavy spring snow".<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Манин|2012|p=296}}</ref>

The thickness of the paint layer on the canvas ''March'' is uneven: relief strokes up to two millimetres thick are used to represent the snow, while the transparent branches of the trees reveal the texture of the canvas.<ref name=":24">{{Harvard citation text|Лужецкая|1965|p=260}}</ref><ref>{{Harvard citation text|Карлсен|Кочик|Виктурина|1963|pp=30–34}}</ref> As one moves away from the foreground, the artist's strokes become less distinct and the treatment more generalised. For the snowy shadows, Levitan used [[Glaze (painting technique)|glaze]] and semi-glaze over a layer of whitewash.<ref name=":24" /> According to the memoirs of the artist Yakov Minchenkov, when Levitan painted the snow on the canvas ''March'', he checked the proportions of [[Chiaroscuro|light and dark]] using photographic images.<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Левитан|1956|p=238}}</ref><ref name=":25">{{Harvard citation text|Минченков|2016|p=4}}</ref> However, according to Minchenkov, “nowhere do you see signs of photography, nowhere did it lead the artist to crude naturalism, did not force him to opt for unnecessary details.”<ref name=":25" />

The paintings ''March'' and ''Golden Autumn'', created in 1895, are considered to be the most significant examples of the influence of [[Impressionism]] on Levitan's work.<ref name=":17" /><ref name=":26">{{Harvard citation text|Круглов|2001|p=15}}</ref><ref name=":27">{{Harvard citation text|Филиппов|2003|p=137}}</ref> ''March'' displays Impressionist characteristics such as "temperamental, open thick strokes, that almost sculpturaly 'mould' the blue March snow."<ref name=":28">{{Harvard citation text|Чурак|2010}}</ref> Relief strokes of whitewash create a sense of snow porosity and contribute to a more active experience of the image.<ref name=":27" /> At the same time, objective techniques are combined with simplicity, demonstrated in the use of certain colours. However, according to art historian Galina Churak, although the pictorial language of the canvas "places Levitan next to the Impressionists", the artist "does not make the decisive step that would allow us to call him an Impressionist".<ref name=":28" /> Comparing ''March'' with "the most Impressionist work" Levitan had created in the 1880s – ''Birch Grove'', art historian Dmitry Sarabianov wrote that in the mid-1890s the artist "did not make significant steps towards the development of the Impressionist system" and "as if stopped at the level of Proto-Impressionism."<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Сарабьянов|1989|pp=294–295}}</ref>

== Reviews ==
In his memoirs, the painter Vasily Baksheev noted that Isaac Levitan remained in his memory as "an artist inseparably connected with the Russian national school of landscape", while "deeply loving the nature of his homeland, tirelessly studying it and embodying it with great skill in his works". According to Baksheev, there is "so much spring warmth, so much light, warming sun" in Levitan's ''March''. Commenting on the painting, Baksheev wrote that he considered it not only one of Levitan's best works, but also "one of the best works of our [(Russian)] school [of painting]". – It was "as much a pearl" as [[Fyodor Vasilyev]]'s ''Thaw'' or [[Alexei Savrasov]]'s ''[[The Rooks Have Returned]].''<ref name=":18" />

Art historian [[Aleksei Fedorov-Davydov|Alexei Fedorov-Davydov]] noted that [[Isaac Levitan|Levitan]] "seldom painted winter and snow in general, preferring to depict its remnants in spring landscapes", but in 1895 he took up such a theme, painting "March", "in which everything breathes a premonition of spring and which is a depiction of a still wintry, sunny day". According to the art historian, "by turning to this new motif, Levitan created a landscape that became a discovery in Russian landscape painting" – "no one before him had painted snow illuminated by the sun in such a colourful and picturesque manner, with blue shadows; no one had depicted the spring sky and trees in such a way." Fedorov-Davydov wrote that "after Levitan, such a motif became a favourite theme in Russian landscape painting,"<ref name=":19" /> citing as examples works such as [[Igor Grabar]]'s ''[[February Azure]]'' and [[Konstantin Yuon]]'s ''March Sun''.<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Фёдоров-Давыдов|1966|p=205}}</ref><ref group="Note">The landscape painter [[Stanislav Zhukovsky]] was also impressed by Levitan's ''March''. He used a similar motif in his painting ''Warmed'' (1899), which was presented at the 27th Travelling Exhibition. However, it was criticised for being an 'obvious imitation' of ''March''.</ref>{{Sfn|Горелов|1982|pp=31—32}}

According to art historian [[Mikhail Alpatov]], the [[Composition (visual arts)|compositional structure]] of Levitan's ''March'' is characterised by its exceptional simplicity, clarity and precision, in which "everything seems simple, natural and even uncomplicated". At the same time, the compositional lines used by the artist give the landscape finality and completeness. According to Alpatov, in ''March'' Levitan formed the image as if from separate fragments "cut by the frame", but at the same time all these parts "form a single whole, a kind of unity." Alpatov wrote that to this landscape "nothing can be added, nothing can be taken away from it" – in none of Levitan's previous works did the artist "find such a happy completeness in nature like near this village house at the edge of the road, at the [[Woodland edge|forest edge]]."<ref name=":22" />

In her book "Plein Air in Russian Painting of the 19th Century", art historian Olga Lyaskovskaya wrote that Levitan's ''March'', like [[Vasily Polenov]]'s ''Moscow Courtyard'', could serve as an example of [[En plein air|plein air]] painting. Lyaskovskaya praised the accuracy of the relations between sky, earth and trees, and the precision with which "the reflections in the snow and the dark blue shadows in the depths" were painted. However, she also noted that the wall of the house and the casement of the open door were not fully completed by the artist: "The pale yellow colour remained a colour and did not become a tone into which the colour of the wall and its change under the influence of sunlight and the surrounding atmosphere should merge". At the same time, according to Lyaskovskaya, the pale trunks of the exposed trees are "excellently painted."<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Лясковская|1966|p=125}}</ref>
[[File:1960 CPA 2465.jpg|left|thumb|230x230px|The painting ''March'' on the [[USSR]] [[postage stamp]] of 1960<ref>{{Cite book |title=Каталог почтовых марок СССР |date=1983 |publisher=Центральное филателистическое агентство «Союзпечать» Министерства связи СССР |volume=1 (1918—1969) |location=Moscow |pages=296 |editor=М.И. Спивак}}</ref>]]
Art historian Faina Maltseva called ''March'' a "great and inspired work" and wrote that it would be difficult to find another landscape in painting of the time that "so reverently conveys the awakening of nature". Noting the brevity of the artistic means used by Levitan to create the canvas, Maltseva wrote that the painting ''March'' presents "a whole and internally complete image, at the same time preserving all the immediacy and freshness of the first impressions."<ref name=":20" /> According to Maltseva, the sunny palette the artist created in this landscape was perceived by his contemporaries as "a discovery in the representation of Russian nature."<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Мальцева|1968|p=126}}</ref>

In a book published in 2001, art historian Vladimir Kruglov wrote that Levitan's ''March'' "has not lost its prominent place, if not in the history of Russian art, then in the souls of people who can feel the beauty of their homeland." According to him, ''March'' established a tradition in Russian painting that has been taken up by a number of artists and continues to this day. Kruglov noted that the successful choice of an almost square canvas format "enhances the impressive expressiveness of the picture", and a short, energetic stroke and lively texture "give a sense of light and air flowing, the play of light and shadow, flickering reflections."<ref name=":26" />

Writing about March, the artist [[Boris Ioganson]] said that he was struck by the "luminous dazzle of the March sun" in this work. According to him, every time he looks at the canvas he stands before this miracle "as if hypnotised", and when he "manages to be in nature in March, or to sit on the boulevard in the city on a sunny March morning, a witty paradox flashes through his mind: "How amazingly nature imitates Levitan's ''March.''"<ref>{{Harvard citation text|Иогансон|1970|p=5}}</ref> According to the literary critic Andrei Turkov, "Levitan's ''March'' seems to capture forever the joyful moment when everything is in front of you, everything is possible."<ref name=":21" />
